Yet here he was, courting partners in Samarkand, a city that epitomizes the historic Persianate realm , whose inhabitants still predominantly speak Tajik , a variant of Persian. The irony was not lost on Iranian diplomats, who took to social media to troll Rubio over the incongruity. Rubio was accompanied by over 200 American businessmen at the summit, where he discussed new trade and investment initiatives. The American-Uzbek Business & Investment Council announced 54 deals worth $12 billion as a result of the visit. As a key hub of the ancient Silk Road, Samarkand is a fitting place to strike trade deals. Rubio spoke of a “fair chance to compete” for American businesses. articles.description: Last week the leaders of the Quad (Quadrilateral Security Dialogue )— comprised of Australia, India, Japan, and the United States — met in the Philippines for the first time in two years. President Donald Trump was in Manila for less than 24 hours with a jam-packed schedule, including his participation in the main event, which was the ASEAN Summit, as well as a bilateral engagement with President Ferdinand Marcos and the Quad summit itself. Perhaps because of this busy itinerary, the Quad was given extremely short shrift, with Trump scheduled to participate for a mere 55 minutes total. But that was only part of the problem. Since the Quad’s last summit in 2024 during President Joe Biden’s administration, the strategic bloc’s members have grown increasingly frustrated with the lack of formal meetings. India is particularly aggrieved because Trump refused to travel to New Delhi when it hosted the Quad last year. Indeed, India still believes that it is the rightful next host of the Quad, even though this year is supposed to be Australia’s turn. articles.title: Where Inflation Is Worst In Europe... And Getting Worse
articles.description: Where Inflation Is Worst In Europe... And Getting Worse Inflation is back above 4% across Europe, and not one of the 21 countries that use the euro is running below the European Central Bank's 2% target . Eurostat's final October figures , released Nov. 18, put annual inflation at 4.0% in both the euro area and the wider EU, up from 3.8% in September and 2.1% a year earlier. The lowest rate in the currency bloc is Malta's 2.3%. Energy prices were 21.0% higher than a year earlier, and energy alone contributed 1.89 percentage points of the 4.0% headline, nearly half of it . Services added 1.55 points, while non-energy industrial goods (0.30) and food, alcohol and tobacco (0.29) barely moved the needle. Inflation rose in 16 member states in October, fell in nine and held steady in two. Source: Visual Capitalist Romania has the highest rate in the EU, at 7.0% , up from 6.5% in September, followed by Lithuania at 6.1% and Bulgaria at 5.9%. Sweden has the lowest, at 0.6%, with Czechia and Denmark next at 2.1% each. articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI review – gaming’s most depraved world is now also its greatest love story
articles.description: With realism that defies belief, this vast game easily accommodates its trademark foulmouthed, OTT chaos – as well as new empathy for the fugitive couple at its centre Tell us: are you playing Grand Theft Auto VI? In GTA VI, Rockstar has created the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen. Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start. If you had been spying on me playing this game over the past few weeks you may well have caught me robbing banks, shooting up a weed farm or tearing along the highway at sunset blaring Bad Bunny on the in-game radio, but you might equally have caught me doing squats at the gym, shopping, assembling a coffee table or walking along the beach eating ice-cream. There is such a multiplicity of things on offer here that it is difficult to nail down what this game definitively is. Is it an interactive crime movie? A city simulator? A driving game? articles.title: Why I love Madrid in winter: ‘Locals get into the spirit by doing their shopping in novelty hats’
articles.description: The streets and squares of the Spanish capital come alive with Madrileños shopping, drinking and dining outdoors, warmed by lap blankets and patio heaters Live in Madrid long enough and you hear the same weather-related proverbs again and again. One old saying goes that the seasons in the Spanish capital break down to “nine months of winter and three months of hell”. And if the city never quite freezes over in the coldest months – except for the blizzard of the century that came with Storm Filomena in 2021 – it is also said that the subtle, evil wind coming in from the mountains could kill a person without snuffing a candle. Personally, I prefer it here at this time of year, though if you’re looking to escape the crowds you might be disappointed. Madrid has only got busier in the 11 years I’ve lived here, and Christmas feels more crowded than midsummer on the central streets around Puerta del Sol. All the main public squares get their own giant Christmas trees, while Plaza de España and Plaza Colón install ice rinks too, and a festive market fills the cobbled core of Plaza Mayor with painted wooden huts. articles.title: Why I love Berlin in winter: ‘Christmas markets arrive in a blaze of twinkling lights’
articles.description: The cold is legendary, but there’s hot chocolate and Glühwein to warm you up, plus crowd-free museums and galleries and cosy candlelit pubs One of the first things Berliners warned me about when I moved here in 2008 was the winters. They talked in hushed, conspiratorial tones about the harsh winds that blew in from the Russian steppes, temperatures of minus 15C and the horrors of frozen bike locks. Having survived 17 of these winters (and counting), and still no hospitalisations for frostbite to report, I can confirm that the warnings, although not necessarily untrue, are not the whole story. Although some Berlin winter days are cold, miserable and grey, they can also be charming, cheerful and chock-full of possibilities. No sooner has the temperature dropped, and the last yellow leaves see-sawed from the trees at the end of November, than the city’s Christmas markets assert themselves in a blaze of twinkling lights, aromatic grill smoke, candied nuts and warming cups of Glühwein. articles.title: Saariaho’s Adriana Mater transcends horror for hope. Female composers are rejecting opera’s legacy of violence | Annilese Miskimmon
articles.description: The death and pain of female characters has always been a bedrock of opera. Kaija Saariaho and today’s female composers are challenging this narrative, and thereby connecting with today’s world In 1992, the Finnish composer Kaija Saariaho saw a Salzburg festival production of Messiaen’s Saint François d’Assise. A series of meditative theological tableaux in which naturalism and plot is secondary to the revelation of deeper spiritual truths, it is now hailed as a masterpiece although it divided critics on its Paris premiere in 1983. Saariaho, one of the painfully few female composers in opera’s 400-year history, recalled thinking: “If that is an opera, then I can write one”. And she did, to notable international acclaim. Her first opera L’Amour de loin (Love from Afar), a tale of medieval courtly love with a libretto by war correspondent and writer Amin Maalouf was premiered, appropriately, at 2000’s Salzburg festival and came to the UK when English National Opera staged it in 2009 . Continue reading...

articles.title: United Strings of Europe review – they’re the intersection in a Venn diagram of chamber music, string orchestra and jazz
articles.description: Wigmore Hall, London Centred around the world premiere of jazz bassist Misha Mullov-Abbado’s almost-concerto, the tight ensemble took a tour of classical fusion and tango fisticuffs In this eclectic programme of mostly 21st-century music, the United Strings of Europe found the intersection in a Venn diagram of chamber music, string orchestra and jazz. At its centre, receiving its world premiere, was The Travelling Violin by the jazz bassist and composer Misha Mullov-Abbado . In four movements, it’s an almost-concerto on an intimate scale. The solo violin, deftly played here by Tamsin Waley-Cohen, has the narrating role, but the writing for the nine supporting string instruments is so intricately woven that it feels like an ensemble piece. It almost seemed strange for Waley-Cohen to give a solo encore at the end, mesmerising though her playing of Nicola Matteis Jr’s A minor Fantasia was. Mullov-Abbado’s piece has a role for jazz bass, which he played himself, and for percussion, from soft-edged shimmering to driving, grooving drums, played by Fred Thomas; the jazz sensibility of both of these leaches into the rest. Led by the violinist Julian Azkoul, the ensemble was tight, churning

articles.title: Possibility couples: how gen Z discovered a new romantic ideal
articles.description: Two-thirds of gen Z daters would rather have a partner who makes them feel hopeful and inspired than one who’s right for them now, according to new research from Hinge Name: Possibility couple. Age: As a term it’s new, having just emerged from Hinge’s 2026 Gen Z DATE report . Continue reading...

articles.title: UK adults: why do you think younger people are having less sex?
articles.description: Over-18s in Britain: share your thoughts on why young and middle-aged people are having sex less frequently than in the past People in Great Britain having less sex – especially young adults Sex among British adults has slumped in recent decades, according to the latest national sexual attitudes survey , with under-45s having half as many monthly encounters as in 1990 and one in three under-25s reporting that they have never had sexual intercourse. The research found the average adult under-45 now has sex twice a month , continuing a downward trend from four times a month in 1990 and three times a month in 2010. Continue reading...

articles.title: Simon Brodkin: ‘Which of my pranks went badly wrong? Well, Boris Johnson became PM after the Theresa May one’
articles.description: The character comedian AKA Lee Nelson handed May a P45 and threw golf balls at Donald Trump. He explains why the pranking’s now on ice – and which funny footballers inspired him How did you get into comedy? I was booted out of every class for making jokes and then I discovered, at medical school, there is such a thing as a career in comedy. I was encouraged by being able to entertain the patients and went straight from that into comedy. Who did you admire when you were starting out? It was always the character comedians: Sacha Baron Cohen, Ricky Gervais, Steve Coogan. On the circuit Al Murray was doing the Pub Landlord. I admired anyone doing characters who could be dropped into multiple situations. As I started doing character comedy myself, I was inspired by people who might not have known how funny they were, such as a big batch of Premier League footballers from Beckham to Gerrard to Rooney. Simon Brodkin: Unleashed is at the Apollo, London , on 13 December and 11 March and on tour in the UK until 26 May Continue reading...

articles.title: Children of the revolution: how the north of England is defining modern men’s fashion
articles.description: Once the historic centre of the textile industry, the north is now home to a host of a provenance-driven labels. But is there a specific northern menswear look? And what does it all mean for the mad-fer-it stereotypes? In 2026, clothing has proved more important to Andy Burnham’s political identity than that of any British prime minister since Margaret Thatcher. He is a loyal Clarks and Adidas wearer, whose Howick worker’s jacket hangs in Manchester’s People’s History Museum. His ousting of Keir Starmer – launched shortly before being photographed jogging in a replica Everton shirt – has been memorialised as the “casual coup”. In one telling, the reason for this is simple: he’s a man from the north. That Burnham is the first born-and-bred northern male PM since Harold Wilson last swished his Gannex raincoat out of Downing Street goes some way to explaining his higher interest in clothing. It’s not necessarily that all men in the south care less about clothing, or that all men in the north do – but that many men from the north express it in such a distinctive, even unified, way. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘It was a cover-up’: HarperCollins accused of using lawyers to shut down concerns about David Walliams
articles.description: Women who spoke to internal investigation about inappropriate behaviour by Walliams still too scared to speak out The publisher HarperCollins used a leading legal firm and a non-disclosure agreement to “cover up” David Walliams’ inappropriate behaviour towards women two years before the children’s author was unexpectedly dropped, according to former staff. Women had complained to the company’s management for years about the author’s alleged misconduct and harassment. The concerns raised included that Walliams had an “inappropriate” sexual relationship with a woman who was an intern when he first met her, had inappropriate interactions with at least three other women connected to the company including asking two for dates, and approached a girl who appeared to be in her teens at a book signing event. Continue reading...

articles.title: More than 300 Russians killed as Moscow props up Mali’s junta, leaked data reveals
articles.description: Exclusive: Records list 349 deaths in three years in Mali and also shed light on Russia’s military activity elsewhere in Africa When the attack on Kidal began before dawn on 25 April this year, the Russian fighters were caught off guard. Within the first hour, checkpoints on the outskirts of the remote desert city nestled among the rocky hills of northern Mali had fallen to the insurgents, who pushed towards the police station where fierce fighting erupted. “Everything was happening at once. Explosions were going off all around us, people were shouting,” recalled a former member of Russia’s Africa Corps who was stationed in Mali at the time and spoke on condition of anonymity. “Nobody knew where the enemy was coming from.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Oceans, fossil fuels and keeping 1.5 alive: the missed opportunities at Cop31
articles.description: The collapse of the ‘Antalya pact’ took away the chance of a unifying effort to deal with a number of issues The “Antalya pact” was supposed to be the keystone document agreed at the UN’s Cop31 climate summit in Turkey, but in the final days and hours countries became entrenched, leaving the pact dead in the water. But what did it say, and what opportunities were missed when it died? Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘The lack of fun is as noticeable as the lack of content’: the reborn Museum of London is all piazza, no punch
articles.description: London Museum Smithfield Why has the revamped museum divided its exhibits into nonsensical themes and shunted all the fascinating stuff downstairs? The results are baffling, unengaging and soulless ‘ An astonishing sight’: Oliver Wainwright reviews the building’s architecture The Museum of London at the Barbican was the capital’s local museum, a crowded and quirky presentation of its history from the Dagenham idol to Vauxhall Pleasure Gardens . But apparently the location deterred casual visitors, and maybe it just wasn’t grand enough to reflect London’s self-conscious significance. For not since ancient Rome has a capital dominated its nation’s history and culture like London. So now we get the rebranded and reimagined London Museum Smithfield. History surrounds you in this neighbourhood: Black Death burials by the Charterhouse, the Knights of St John, the Smithfield martyrs, William Wallace’s execution site. So goodbye scruffy brutalist Slough House location, hello deep history. Except when you enter the new museum, all that history, all those layers going back to the Romans and earlier, have been brushed away. If you want an illustration that bigger is not better, this is it. Wh

articles.title: Who needs perfume? The incredible link between body odour and relationships that last
articles.description: The longer you have been with your partner, the more likely you are to find their natural scent arousing, according to a study from Radboud University in the Netherlands Name: Body odour. Age: Everyone has always smelled of something. Continue reading...

articles.title: I don’t have children. A stranger decided I was ruining my life
articles.description: A reader sent me unsolicited photos of his children, insisting I was missing out on everything. Why are other people’s reproductive choices so threatening to many of us? Last fall, a man I had never met wrote to inform me that my fertility window was “rapidly closing” – and that I couldn’t possibly be happy. What had prompted this unsolicited assessment was an article I had published about how fascist regimes seek to control women’s roles in society. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘An extravagantly illuminated beast’: the best artificial Christmas trees in the UK – tested
articles.description: Pick wisely, and your fake fir could be reused for decades of Decembers. From pre-lit to frosted to space-saving, here are our festive favourites • The best beauty Advent calendars • The best Christmas baubles In the 70s and 80s Essex of my youth, no one had a real Christmas tree unless they lived in the country, or perhaps Loughton. Our family’s skinny artificial tree is now 55 years old and comes out every year at my sister’s. It’s shed a few plastic “needles” down the years, but it’s still standing proud – which is more than you can say for a real Christmas tree bought in 1971, or even 2025. Therein lies the surprising environmental efficiency of artificial Christmas trees. The Carbon Trust says using a fake tree over seven to 20 years (depending on its weight and materials) can create fewer emissions than buying a new, commercially grown tree every year. The key is to buy an artificial tree you’ll love enough to roll out for decades. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘The icing on the cake’: how Nigella saved Bake Off
articles.description: Viewing figures are up and the new judge has spiced up the show with her wit, charm and articulate appreciation of doughy delights. The stale previous seasons are fast becoming a mere memory When Nigella Lawson helps crown the new champion of The Great British Bake Off on Tuesday night, two other winners will also be celebrating: the show itself and broadcaster Channel 4. The fabled “Nigella effect” has freshened up a franchise that was beginning to taste distinctly stale. Having replaced Prue Leith as judge for this 17th edition, alongside the ever-present Paul Hollywood, the domestic goddess has made the cake-making contest essential viewing again. Prompting a public outpouring of love, magisterial Lawson has proved the missing ingredient in the show’s resurgence. Continue reading...

articles.title: Sir Stanley Wells obituary
articles.description: Eminent Shakespeare scholar and author who brought together the worlds of academia and the theatre In 1978 Oxford University Press made Stanley Wells, who has died aged 96, director of a Shakespeare department specially created so that he could produce a new edition of the complete works. Starting from scratch, he went back to the early printed copies, the quartos and folios, and thought through every editorial and textual decision – how to modernise the spelling and punctuation, and edit stage directions and speakers’ names, while giving the rationales for emendations. The single volume Complete Shakespeare appeared in 1986, edited by Stanley, with Gary Taylor, John Jowett and William Montgomery. It proved to be groundbreaking, startling and controversial. Continue reading...

articles.title: From Sovereigns to Servants by Alexandra Prokopenko review – Putin and his yes men
articles.description: A disturbing account of the way Russia’s elites have reduced themselves to craven courtiers When Vladimir Putin launched his full-scale invasion of Ukraine four and a half years ago, it was a shock, but it wasn’t a surprise. The US and the UK had been publicly warning their allies for weeks about what Russia was planning, as well as threatening the Russians with a wave of sanctions unprecedented against a major power. Putin’s foreign policy had long relied on confusion and untruth. By saying that they knew exactly what he was up to, Britain and America were hoping first to deny him his usual ambiguity, and second to pressure the men around him into making him stop, since war would deprive them of the stolen assets they’d stashed in London’s most exclusive neighbourhoods. Continue reading...

articles.title: Man Theft Auto – why did so few women review GTA VI, the biggest video game of the decade?
articles.description: Given that this is the first Grand Theft Auto in 30 years with a female protagonist, you might have expected to hear from female critics. But you would have expected mostly in vain Grand Theft Auto VI is now the biggest video game launch of all time, and is likely to become the biggest video game of all time. It’s a once-in-a-lifetime event, a phenomenon that will shape games as a medium and pop culture at large for years to come, set against the backdrop of its developers fighting for their rights at studio Rockstar Games . It has snatched sales and streaming records and become the best-reviewed game ever (pulling ahead of 1998’s The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time). It’s also the first GTA game with a female protagonist, who also happens to be a woman of colour. Yet very few women (and seemingly no women of colour) played and reviewed it before release. When GTA VI’s review embargo lifted on 18 November, the gender imbalance was immediately obvious. Out of 156 reviewers, only six appeared to be women. As journalist Lex Luddy noted in a BlueSky post , that is 3.8%. Continue reading...

articles.title: GTA VI’s jaw-dropping success: in figures
articles.description: Content creators have produced hundreds of millions of hours of video game since its launch Grand Theft Auto ( GTA) VI became the largest video game release of all time last week and while it is hard to say exactly how many people are playing the game (current estimates say at least 30 million), there are plenty of other jaw-dropping data points we do know. Data on streaming the game suggests that only two days into its release a cumulative 364.5m hours have been watched – roughly 41,000 years of content. Put another way, that translates to more than 41,000 years worth of people riffling through cash registers, hanging drywall, birding, diving or hijacking jets. That’s according to streaming data from Streams Charts, a data and analytics company that has been tracking Rockstar Game’s long-awaited title. Continue reading...

articles.title: What happened when the man who took a million photographs embraced colour?
articles.description: The Photographers’ Gallery, London Sanlé Sory is known for his black and white images taken during independence in Burkina Faso – but his colour portraits bring humour, insouciance and joy Despite his wide renown, there have been hardly any major exhibitions of Sanlé Sory’s work. His last UK show was in 2019, concentrating on the black-and-white images the Burkinabé photographer made in the first two decades after opening his own studio, Volta Photo, in Bobo-Dioulasso in 1960 – a period that coincided with the first two decades of independence in Burkina Faso. This new Photographer’s Gallery show shifts the focus to the 1980s and 1990s, when Sory began working in colour. It’s easy to see why, even with few exhibitions, Sory has made such an impression on audiences. There are the familiar west African studio photography tropes westerners love, where sound, image, fashion and pose collide. The props are popping, the style is irrepressible, the energy is irresistible. I wonder if Sory’s speed and instinct came from the time he spent early in his career racing on his motorbike to photograph car accidents for newspapers and the police. These portraits are the opposite of a car crash, th

articles.title: RPO/Hisaishi review – Studio Ghibli’s genius brings his concerto to a rapt London
articles.description: Royal Albert Hall, London The Royal Philharmonic rode the bucking rhythms of the star composer’s intricate score, the highlight of an evening that also included works by Steve Reich and David Lang If anyone tells you that classical music is dead you need just two words to refute them: Joe Hisaishi. The 75-year-old Japanese conductor, composer and pianist may be best known for his soundtracks, particularly his long association with Hayao Miyazaki’s Studio Ghibli films, but has parlayed his popular success into serious concert-hall credentials. You can debate style and genre, but there’s no arguing with the impact of a man who can sell out the Royal Albert Hall on a Monday night in November with an evening of music by Steve Reich, David Lang and Hisaishi himself – and not a film score in sight. Continue reading...

articles.title: Puzzles and games are finally all in one place
articles.description: The latest updates on our trivia, logic, word and number games, as explained by our new octopod mascot, Ink The Guardian finally has an online home for its puzzles and games , to go with the dedicated puzzles section in our app. We’re planning to expand the number of puzzles we offer over the coming weeks and months, with more trivia, logic, word and number games in the works. Here to explain the changes is Ink , an octopus who has just started his new role as the Guardian’s puzzles and games mascot. Hand instructions to actors (6) Shopper set out – female with a good idea of what is in store (10) Continue reading...

articles.title: The secret to the perfect Christmas party cocktail
articles.description: Festive drinks are all about capturing the warmth and theatre of the season, so lean into wintry flavours such as orange and cloves, and add a bit of drama by bringing out the blowtorch What are the best cocktails to make for a Christmas party? Dan, by email We’re all in favour of getting the party season started early, Dan, so now is as good a time as any to get your drinks cupboard in order. “Ultimately, Christmas cocktails are all about bringing a little warmth, nostalgia and theatre, so don’t be afraid to have fun with seasonal flavours,” says Josie Pink, author of River Cottage: Cocktails and Botanicals . The smell of orange, be it fresh or dried, is never too far away at this time of year, and one reason Pink suggests having a batch of orange liquor on hand, not least “to rustle up a margarita or two”. Ditto dried citrus wheels: “They’re a must,” she says. “Not only are they gorgeous for adorning cocktails, but any misshapes can be turned into marmalade dust, and any spares into home decorations.” Pink also advises getting some syrups in your arsenal – “I’d opt for a batch of trusty vanilla syrup” – plus a chai number “for those fragrant, warming spice flavours that we all as

articles.title: Morrisons trip cost me £100 in parking charges
articles.description: Euro Car Parks insists my vehicle was there for more than 13 hours because its ANPR cameras missed my exit A recent shopping trip to Morrisons cost me £100 in parking charges because its car park operator insists I never left. I’d visited the store twice that day, once at 8am and then late that evening. Continue reading...

articles.title: Was Benjamin Franklin the original wellness bro? I lived like him for a day to find out
articles.description: Before online influencers existed, the founding father published an annual wellness pamphlet. I followed his 13 virtues he found necessary for a good life Benjamin Franklin doesn’t get enough credit. Yes, he was a founding father of the United States; he invented the lightning rod and his face is printed on $100 bills. But rarely is he celebrated for his contributions to the most meaningful field of human achievement: wellness influencing. Centuries before GRWM videos and scientifically dubious podcasts were a dollar-sign-shaped glint in their creators’ eyes, Franklin was doling out life advice. Under the pseudonym Poor Richard, Franklin published an annual pamphlet and minted maxims like “Diligence is the mother of good luck” and “Fish and visitors stink after three days.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Caffeine has crept into everything. With all the buzz, are we at risk of too much of a high? | Antiviral
articles.description: We are offered a seemingly endless array of drinks and foods that now come with the world’s most consumed psychoactive drug Read more in the Antiviral series Feeling tired and need a pick-me-up but finding your morning cup of coffee isn’t touching the sides? Instead of the predictable choice (a second coffee), you could instead opt for a seemingly endless array of other drinks and foods that now come with added caffeine. You might energise yourself before your morning gym session with a few caffeinated scoops of a pre-workout supplement. Afterwards, you could refuel with a caffeinated protein shake or a protein bar with added guarana – whose seeds contain caffeine. Continue reading...

articles.title: Share a tip on your best European travel discovery of 2026
articles.description: Tell us about your favourite travel find of the year – the best tip wins £200 towards a Coolstays break It’s often the surprise or unexpected discoveries from our travels that stick in the mind long after we’ve returned home. Perhaps it was an under-the-radar museum, a pretty mountain village, an outstanding little hotel, a hidden beach or an amazing hiking trail. We’d love to hear about your favourite travel discovery of 2026 in Europe, including the UK. The best tip of the week, chosen by Tom Hall of Lonely Planet , wins a £200 voucher to stay at a Coolstays property – the company has more than 3,000 worldwide. The best tips will appear in the Guardian Travel section and website. Continue reading...

articles.title: Why I love Rome in winter: ‘We reclaim the city and slip back into familiar routines’
articles.description: There is plenty of sunshine, the tourists have thinned out – and no one does a traditional Christmas like the Romans There was a time when, during a Rome winter, I would crave the warmer months. Not any more. The combination of intense heat and overtourism has made summer poco piacevole , as Italians would say – not very pleasant. So come mid-September, when the temperature drops and the crowds thin out, our mood lifts as we reclaim the city and slip back into familiar routines. In winter, the temperature is mostly mild and there is still plenty of sunshine (we do tend to grumble if the rain and grey skies persist for a few days). Rome is best seen on foot, and my favourite time to walk it is on a Sunday. Until earlier this year, I lived in Esquilino, a vibrant neighbourhood close to Termini train station. I’d begin with coffee at Gatsby Cafe by Piazza Vittorio before walking along Via Merulana – a tree-lined street similar to a Parisian boulevard – and then through the Colle Oppio park, past the Colosseum and towards Circo Massimo . Continue reading...

articles.title: The pest I’ll never forget: the cockerel whose crowing almost destroyed me
articles.description: When a neighbour installed a braying bird on the roof of our block of flats, the noise was relentless from sunrise till sunset. It became the sinister soundtrack to my life You can’t choose your family or your colleagues. And you definitely can’t choose your neighbours: the people with whom you involuntarily share a postcode and the ritual of swapping misdelivered Amazon parcels. For the most part, the neighbours in my block of flats are reassuringly neighbourly. During lockdown, I became unofficial IT support for one trying to home-school her son. I spent years emailing a PR man about Guardian celebrity interviews without realising he lived two doors away. And one of my neighbours (and now my hero) used to be in the 80s punk band Splodgenessabounds, who sang Two Pints of Lager and a Packet of Crisps Please. The other half I couldn’t pick out of a police lineup, although I certainly know their habits, from the phantom non-recycler who bungs all their plastic bottles and newspapers in the normal black bin, to the mystery resident who happily leaves the security gate open. But the one that is lodged most firmly in my memory is the neighbour who, last year, kept a pet cockerel on the

articles.title: Houseplant hacks: does grouping plants together increase humidity?
articles.description: It will help during winter months, but there are better solutions for really thirsty plants The problem With the onset of winter, the heating comes on, humidity drops and tropical plants that yearn for rainforest conditions end up in something closer to a desert. Cue crispy leaf edges. Humidifiers work, but they require buying, filling and cleaning. Misting works, but you need to remember to do it. So, a free, lazy alternative has an obvious appeal. The hack This hack is based on transpiration. Plants constantly release water vapour through their leaves, so huddling them together raises the humidity around them. Continue reading...

articles.title: Country diary: A close watch on this autumn’s leaf fall – it’s been unpredictable | Elizabeth-Jane Burnett
articles.description: Creedy Valley, Devon: Three oaks in a row – one is green, one is bronze and the other is shedding its golden leaves like a shaken snow globe Leaves fall from the oak on the brow of the hill in a flurry. There is only a slight wind, yet it is as though a snow globe has been shaken – so many leaves are animated. The process seems to take a long time. Mesmerised, I follow as they glitter to the ground. There are oaks on either side of this one. To the right, despite its close proximity, the tree has not felt the same call to let its leaves go. Instead, it holds them close – a burnished bronze, brighter even than its neighbour’s gold. To the left, a greener tree stands on the end of the line. Continue reading...

articles.title: Have you downloaded Meta’s AI assistant Muse or do you plan to?
articles.description: The digital butler, which can go shopping on behalf of users, is available in the US, UK and Canada. What do you think about it? Meta is continuing its rollout of its Muse AI assistant, with the UK the latest country where the digital butler will be available to go shopping, book tickets and carry out negotiations on a user’s behalf. The Facebook-owner’s app has been a hit in the US, where it is ranked first and second respectively on Google and Apple’s free app store, and has also launched in Canada. The assistant comes with a cuddly avatar as default, but users are invited to give it a name, look and a personality. Continue reading...

articles.title: Do you enjoy playing board games as an adult? We’d like to hear from you
articles.description: We would like to hear from young people who play board games. What do you play and why do you enjoy them? Are you a triple-scoring Scrabble addict or perhaps you’re more of a Monopoly player? Board games have grown in popularity among younger adults in recent years, with games nights offering a welcome, screen-free social activity. Continue reading...

articles.title: Men have used wealth and fame to get away with abuse. No longer | Andy Burnham
articles.description: The NDAs that enforce silence, the behaviour that exploits the age of consent. I'll address both with sweeping changes to keep women and girls safe Burnham opens door to wider NDAs ban at ‘watershed moment’ on abuse Powerful men using their fame and money to silence anyone who calls out their behaviour. Victims treated as though they’re the ones who’ve done something wrong. And a culture where abuse can hide in plain sight because people in positions of power think they can get away with it. That’s what we’ve seen in the past few weeks. This must be a watershed moment. Not just for the culture of the entertainment industry but for us as a nation. Things have improved in the past decade or so, but we are still far from being where we need to be for women and girls to feel safe and be safe. Sadly, many women and girls will find the recent stories all too close to home, whether it’s casual disrespect in the workplace, undermining “jokes”, or being told they are somehow at fault for something that has happened to them. Continue reading...

articles.title: Shop small, save big: 21 brilliant Black Friday bargains from UK independents
articles.description: From farm-to-table hot sauce to handwoven blankets, here are our favourite discounts from bricks-and-mortar shops and indie retailers • The best Black Friday deals Listen: we love a discounted air fryer as much as the next person, but there’s no doubt shopping for Black Friday deals can feel a bit … icky. From handing even more of your cash to global corporations to the suspicion you’re adding to a mass of plastic floating somewhere in the Antarctic, it’s no wonder a third of Britons say they hate Black Friday. But there is a way of having your discounted jacket and wearing it too. And that’s by shopping with local and independent retailers. Many wonderful bricks-and-mortar shops and small online retailers around the UK take part in Black Friday, often in creative and fun ways. Continue reading...

articles.title: Metropolitan police still institutionally racist and misogynist, says report
articles.description: Independent review finds force has ‘fundamental systemic issues’ three years after damning report on Sarah Everard murder Latest review of Met police culture finds little has changed since last one The Metropolitan police remain institutionally racist, misogynistic and homophobic three years after a damning review into the force’s culture, a report has found. The investigation by Gillian Fairfield found “fundamental, systemic issues” and “institutional defensiveness” still existed in Britain’s biggest police force, which has struggled “to acknowledge racism as a structural problem”. Continue reading...

articles.title: Burnham opens door to wider NDAs ban at ‘watershed moment’ on abuse
articles.description: PM brings forward changes to non-disclosure agreements and promises consultation on staggered age of consent Men have used wealth and fame to get away with abuse. No longer Andy Burnham has called recent high-profile rape trials a “watershed moment” for the UK and has opened the door to a wider ban on non-disclosure agreements. The prime minister has brought forward changes to NDAs so that from January victims of crimes or workplace harassment will have complete freedom over who they can speak to, even if they have signed an NDA, and he promised the move was “just the start” of a crackdown. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Not about notches on bedpost’: people in Great Britain having less sex – especially young adults
articles.description: Lancet survey shows under-45s have sex twice a month – down from four times in 1990 – and one in three under-25s have never had intercourse UK adults: tell us why you think younger people are having less sex Sex among British adults has slumped in recent decades, with under-45s having half as many monthly encounters as in 1990 and one in three under-25s reporting that they have never had sexual intercourse. The fourth National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles, or Natsal, found the average adult under 45 now has sex twice a month , continuing a downward trend from four times a month in 1990 and three times a month in 2010. Continue reading...

articles.title: Why is France fighting Vanuatu over two uninhabited islands in the Pacific?
articles.description: The battle over the Matthew and Hunter islands – and their 350,000 sq km economic zone – has made its way to the UN’s highest court Two tiny specks of volcanic land in the vast Pacific Ocean – home to seabirds and not much else – are at the centre of an escalating territorial battle between France and Vanuatu. The decades-long dispute over the Matthew and Hunter islands has entered a new phase, with Vanuatu launching two separate international legal proceedings against France as part of its attempt to claim these Pacific territories. Arbitration proceedings began last month, which could threaten France’s claim to a vast expanse of the ocean surrounding the islands. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Guardian view on disability benefits: Timms’s radical review is rooted in experience | Editorial
articles.description: Ministers have taken on board their MPs’ message about cuts. Now anxious claimants need reassurance Four million people with disabilities or long‑term health conditions in the UK claim personal independence payment (Pip). A review by Sir Stephen Timms, the social security minister, offers a blueprint for how to overhaul it . Its recommendations pose a difficult question for ministers: are they prepared to meet the needs that a more accurate assessment of the costs of disability might reveal? Sir Stephen worked as one of three co-chairs with a steering group of 12 people with a range of professional and lived experience. There is broad agreement that Pip needs to be reformed. The announcement on Tuesday that the government would accept the recommendation of a new fast track for claimants whose conditions are lifelong or unlikely to improve, and abolish unnecessary benefit reviews, signalled that ministers are ready for change. The decision, affecting one in 10 claimants in England and Wales, is welcome but long overdue. Ministers should work with the devolved administrations to ensure similar progress elsewhere in the UK. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Guardian view on Andy Burnham and Wales: a devolution blindspot at No 10 | Editorial
articles.description: The PM has summarily dismissed Welsh demands for further powers similar to those enjoyed in Scotland. The approach seems at odds with his consensual style As he headed for Downing Street this summer, Andy Burnham said that he aimed to be “as collaborative and pragmatic as possible” in his dealings with the governments of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. His predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, had notoriously warned ministers against being “overly deferential” in discussions with the devolved administrations. But Mr Burnham’s signature commitment to distributing more power and responsibility out of Westminster, and his consensual style, appeared to augur well for a positive reset in relations. In Wales, this early optimism has just been brutally quashed by an uncharacteristically peremptory letter from Mr Burnham to the first minister, Rhun ap Iorwerth. In it, the prime minister flatly rejected Welsh calls for the devolving of powers in relation to policing and justice, the crown estate and rail infrastructure. In the case of policing, Mr Burnham is in the curious position of denying to Mr ap Iorwerth the type of power that he enjoyed as the mayor of Greater Manchester. Do you have

articles.title: Neets and needs: a loss of focus on harmful life experiences | Letters
articles.description: Dr Sebastian Kraemer on the Sure Start programme and the effect of the ‘diagnostic revolution’, a parent of three young adults on gaps in Alan Milburn’s proposals, and Prof Geeta Nargund on how the NHS could develop young local talent Mark Mon-Williams praises Peter Fonagy’s emphasis on needs-led mental health care, while mourning the loss of Sure Start and cuts in health visitors ( Childhood neglect, unmet needs, mental health struggles: this is the making of a Neet, 18 November ). Mon-Williams’ article also chronicles intergenerational neglect by disconnection: a mother can’t afford to travel to an antenatal class, then information following her premature baby daughter’s NHS care is not shared with social and educational services; she is effectively excluded from a school with an outstanding Ofsted rating and joins the ranks of those not in employment, education or training (Neet). articles.title: Backward steps for police on participation in Pride marches and anti-racism | Letters
articles.description: Shabana Mahmood’s ‘new impartiality standard’ for police is not non-political, argues Chris Sinha . Plus a letter from Dr Peter Purton The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, says police in uniform should not participate in LGBTQ+ pride events, saying that “at those marches, you will often have campaigners, on gender identity … and those issues are now contested … the marching alongside looks like a political act” ( Shabana Mahmood backs ban on police marching in pride events in uniform, 18 November ). She also said that it is wrong for the police not to be colour-blind in policing, as in the previous anti-racism commitment – a commitment that reflected the recognition of the history of systemic racism, and of the perceptions of the police by communities who are policed – and that the police should not engage with “activist groups and campaigners”. articles.title: Gordon Brown’s ideas on zero-sum beliefs don’t add up | Letters
articles.description: The former Labour prime minister is wrong to dismiss all zero-sum thinking as misguided, writes Gavin Bailey The broad thrust of Gordon Brown’s argument is correct ( The far right is menacing Europe – but it is fragile. What the extremists and voters want isn’t the same, 22 November ). However, he is wrong to suggest that zero-sum beliefs are erroneous. Many things in life are zero-sum. If I own a house, you can’t also own it; if I burn some gas to heat it, you can’t use the same gas. If the UK makes all the cars for the European market, other countries’ carmakers won’t be making them. Yes, growth can come from collaboration and trade, but the proceeds are not infinite and take time to achieve. Continue reading...

articles.title: Why white-tailed sea eagles are a danger to Britain’s seabirds | Letters
articles.description: The reintroduction of the birds in England and Wales spells disaster for fragile marine ecosystems, warns Tim Birkhead Your article on white-tailed sea eagle reintroduction ( Reintroduction of white-tailed eagles puts seabird colonies at risk of wipeout, say experts, 8 November ) highlighted the risk that white-tailed sea eagles are likely to pose to Britain’s seabirds. To argue, as Prof Ian Convery and Rebecca Wrigley did in their responses ( Letters, 15 November ), that the re-establishment of white-tailed sea eagles will somehow restore a lost paradise is fallacious. Where is the evidence that sea eagles will restore that balance? There is no evidence. Also, suggesting that because in the distant past sea eagles and seabirds coexisted, their reintroduction will pose no problems is naive. By failing to acknowledge that past marine ecosystems were much more robust, and seabird prey more abundant, than they are today, these two authors miss the point that it is precisely because our seabirds are currently short of food that they are so vulnerable to disturbance and predation from white-tailed sea eagles. Continue reading...

articles.title: Blade Runner 2099 review – every scene of this TV version is packed with terrifying visual beauty
articles.description: In this adaptation of the sci-fi franchise Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer are on a quest to track down a group of replicants gone rogue. It’s a neon-filled world of beautiful doomsday visions Memory: the mother of the muses, and the heart of the Blade Runner franchise. Science fiction is forever asking what it means to be human and, in the future dystopia first painted by Ridley Scott’s 1982 movie, the answer is that we are what we remember: we are the experiences we preserve as a collection of short films inside our heads. In the original Blade Runner, Rachael (Sean Young) is devastated to learn that her childhood memories aren’t real, and she is therefore a robot “replicant”; in Denis Villeneuve’s sequel, Blade Runner 2049, K (Ryan Gosling) knows he’s a replicant but hopes his memories are a sign that he is something close to human. Blade Runner has always been relevant to the age of AI, in that its starting point is that enslaved robots have rebelled. But the new version, the story’s first expansion into television, is acutely topical in an era where we’re increasingly anxious about whether what we’re seeing – or reading – is the work of machines. Fifty years on from the event

articles.title: The story of how Pelé and Maradona went from friends to bitter rivals
articles.description: A new book charts the complicated relationship between the two legends, starting on a sunny afternoon in Rio in 1979 Pelé and Diego Maradona first met in April 1979, not long after the Argentinian led his country’s under-20 side to the finals of the World Youth Cup. Maradona told a journalist friend that his dream was to meet the Brazilian, and after a few weeks of aborted attempts to bring them together – mostly because Diego did not want to travel on a Monday, the one day he had free for his girlfriend Claudia – the meeting finally took place in Rio. Reporter Guillermo Blanco, who was writing about the meeting for Argentinian sports magazine El Gráfico, got the OK from Pelé’s people and was so intent on making it happen that he checked Maradona onto a flight one Sunday night without telling him. He collared the young man after Argentine Juniors played Huracán and then raced to the airport and put him on a plane with his father, his agent and a photographer. Continue reading...

articles.title: What’s the most sustainable way to eat fish? Forget it. There isn’t one | George Monbiot
articles.description: Don’t take the bait offered up by ‘conservation’ charities. Fishing is about as good for our ecosystems as tobacco is for our health Drumroll please. I am about to unveil the species of fish that’s best to eat if you want to protect the living seas. Ta-dah! It’s … I hope that clears things up. Unfortunately, over the past few years, a noisy industry has developed to tell you otherwise. You’re doing the planet a favour if you eat mackerel , sorry, cod, I mean haddock, no coley, make that pollack – oh, whoops! These choices might make you feel better about yourself. But they do nothing but harm to marine wildlife. The fish you should choose is none of the above. Cause, could I introduce you to effect? In April, the Marine Conservation Society, through its Good Fish Guide, suggested you stop eating cod and eat hake instead . Six months later, it lamented that hake is now overexploited thanks to “increased fishing pressure” , and downgraded its sustainability ratings. How on earth did that happen? Beats me. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Half price!’ ‘Only two left!’ How to resist the bargains you just don’t need – this Black Friday and beyond
articles.description: Everywhere you look, there’s another unrepeatable deal at an unmissable price. What’s on offer will make you happier, smarter and sexier. Except, of course, it won’t. Let us help you ignore the ‘consumption noise’ The other morning a parcel arrived and I was momentarily mystified by its contents. Peering at what appeared to be a shiny maroon and pink cushion cover, the penny eventually dropped. It was the fancy “Sweat Bag” I had bought on impulse when it popped up on Instagram after a particularly trying day. The blurb had convinced me it was the perfect solution for storing sweaty gym gear, ensuring that everything else in my bag remained pristine. “Whether it’s a 6am class before work or squeezing in lunchtime workouts, the Sweat Bag moves with you, wherever your day takes you.” I liked the idea of being this busy, efficient human, but in reality, I generally head straight home after my workouts and collapse beside the nearest biscuit tin. I had no business spending, ahem, £39 on it. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘I was physically beating myself up before a take’: Rory Culkin on anxiety, fatherhood and his famous brothers
articles.description: The star of Lords of Chaos, Scream 4 and Gabriel was always drawn to the dark side. Is that why he seems happier in Hollywood than his better-known brothers – and why he loved making Nocturne with Stephen Graham? Rory Culkin is enjoying the autumn afternoon in a Manhattan park. The trees are a dazzling blur of yellows, greens, oranges and reds; the background silence is so pure you can hear it. “I’m here with my baby daughter, Havoc,” he says. “Havoc Moon.” I tell him that is the spookiest name ever. “Thank you,” he says. Culkin chuckles like a revving moped, his huge blue eyes lighting up. “Yes, it’s a weird one. I think she’ll probably be the opposite. A sweet, quiet girl. She’ll play a harp or something.” He explains its origin. “I just threw out names to my partner one night when we went to dinner. She wasn’t taking to anything. I then suggested Havoc, and she really liked it. She came up with the Moon part. When we got home there was fresh graffiti on the wall across the street saying ‘Havoc’, and I was like: ‘That is a sign from the gods – we’ve got to do it.’” Continue reading...

articles.title: Ghost strikes: the new drone superpowers raining death from above
articles.description: The spread of cheap drones means warfare is increasingly conducted by invisible armies at the push of a button. He did not even know who had carried out the killing, or under which authority – several nations have drones patrolling the skies of Somalia looking for Islamic State militants, including the US, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Turkey and the Somali government. articles.title: ‘The whole process just doesn’t work’: claimants relive the agonies of Pip assessments
articles.description: Applicants recount a catalogue of problems including tedious award reviews for sufferers of severe lifelong conditions Rob Denholm clearly remembers his first personal independence payment (Pip) assessment, when he was asked more than 90 questions in 55 minutes. “You’re constantly asked the same question in a different way. I remember thinking, I must not have answered that properly, so you try and find a different way to answer. And by doing that, you’re working against yourself,” he said. “The assessor didn’t know about my cognitive impairment, and I couldn’t find the words to explain.” Continue reading...
