articles.title: Reeling in the years: how Hollywood fell for its own vanishing glories
articles.description: The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is the latest in a growing wave of movies steeped in nostalgia for a heyday in stark contrast to its current ruination If Los Angeles was a person, it might just be a laid-back fiftysomething trouper with cool sunglasses and an even better haircut. Some dodgy episodes in his past, but still handles himself with style. In other words, Los Angeles personified is Cliff Booth – the over-the-hill stuntman played by Brad Pitt in Once Upon a Time … in Hollywood , now turned studio fixer in the sequel, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth. Set eight years later in 1977, Further Mis-Adventures is more plot-driven, more Elmore Leonard-esque than the pure expansive “memory piece” of Once Upon a Time. But both films are steeped in the ambience and lore of old LA, drawn in part from Quentin Tarantino’s memories of cruising around the streets aged six in his stepdad’s Karmann Ghia (the car Booth also drives). They’re part of the recent intensely nostalgic LA revivalist mini-boom of work that also includes Paul Thomas Anderson’s Licorice Pizza (2021), Damien Chazelle’s Babylon (2022) and Ti West’s MaXXXine (2024). Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘I said no thanks to the casting couch. But other actresses had problems’: Jane Alexander on 50 years of stardom
articles.description: The Great White Hope, All the President’s Men, Kramer vs Kramer … Alexander has a CV most actors can only dream of. She talks us through the highs and lows – including a ‘beautiful’ encounter with Muhammad Ali Jane Alexander will never forget the play that won her a Tony award, a husband and her first film role. The Great White Hope, which ran on Broadway from 1968 to 1970, was based on the life of Black boxer Jack Johnson, who in 1908 became world heavyweight champion in segregated America. Alexander played Eleanor, a white woman married to an African American boxer also called Jack, at a time when interracial marriages were still illegal in many states. Decades later, when the play opened, the US supreme court had only recently struck down all remaining bans – and Alexander received hate mail and death threats for the role. Continue reading...

articles.title: Mow down an alligator to the music of Mahler! I love how Grand Theft Auto VI went crazy for classical
articles.description: Rob a bank to the sound of Sibelius, steal a chopper listening to Liszt … piano sensation Yuja Wang is one of the surprise treats of GTA VI – and her thrilling musical choices made me crash into a G-Wagen I blame Yuja Wang for crashing my car. You know how it is, you’re cruising as fast you can on the freeway, listening to Symphony FM. And then DJ Yuja says: “It’s afternoon here in Vice City: for the worst of you, the day is just starting. Maybe the next piece will inspire you to turn your life around.” And then she played Tchaikovsky – the finale of the Fifth Symphony – and I just lost it to the music. The energy and tempest of the finale turned me into a driving maniac, and I ended up crashing into a G-Wagen down a one-way street as the minor-key maelstrom took over. Thanks Yuja. I’ll send you the repair bill. Such are the hazards of discovering that among the 24 stations you can listen to in Grand Theft Auto VI – and not only in your car – is Symphony FM, hosted by the in-game Yuja, who really is the real-life piano superstar Yuja Wang . And in choosing her “favourite pieces and curating a playlist for players to discover”, she’s put together a set of 16 pieces that only she cou

articles.title: Secrets by Bob Woodward review – the world’s most famous reporter reveals all
articles.description: The journalist who helped bring down Nixon on false starts, Watergate, and the art of cultivating a source ‘I have always disliked the term ‘investigative reporter’.” So writes Bob Woodward, one of the most celebrated reporters of our time – the man whose Watergate reporting with Carl Bernstein undoubtedly changed the US presidency and journalism itself for ever. His longtime boss, the Washington Post editor Ben Bradlee, disliked the term too: “All reporting is investigative,” Bradlee would say. The term conjures a certain sophistication, perhaps, but part of the beauty of a reporter’s work is how deceptively unsophisticated it can be. Secrets is a far-ranging, revealing memoir of an extraordinary career, but more than that, it is an ode to grinding it out – knocking on doors, asking and asking again, listening, taking notes, making notes on the notes, patiently following every lead to exhaustion. In a media ecosystem saturated with fast and flimsy takes, this feels like a tonic. The real star of his story, Woodward seems to insist, is the shoe leather. Continue reading...

articles.title: Caitlin Moran on Radiohead, anxiety and the perfect baked potato | Comfort Eating
articles.description: Caitlin brings her ultimate comfort food to the table: a celebration of carbs and dairy. From teenage music journalist to bestselling feminist author, Caitlin Moran has spent her life asking questions, challenging convention and making us laugh along the way. She's interviewed rock stars, changed the conversation around feminism and written some of the funniest observations about modern life.  She reveals what it was like growing up as the eldest of eight children in a home-schooled, unconventional family, learning to cook from library books. She also looks back on her teenage years as a music journalist, touring with the likes of Radiohead and the Beastie Boys, her early experiences of fame and the making of How to Be a Woman. Plus, she opens up about her relationship with food and body image, and how she came to recognise and eventually let go of the anxiety she once thought was essential to her creativity. New episodes of Comfort Eating with Siobhán are out every Wednesday.  Continue reading...

articles.title: Still racist, misogynistic and homophobic. I’m putting Britain’s biggest police force on notice – we won’t tolerate this | Sadiq Khan
articles.description: Another day and, despite all the promises, another damning report on the Met. There will be a reset: the public won’t be brushed off any more and neither will I In March 2023, Baroness Louise Casey published her damning review into the Metropolitan police. The review – which I commissioned after a series of appalling scandals – called for systemic reform to a failing organisation unable to tackle the profound problems it faced. But yesterday’s independent follow-up report by Dr Gillian Fairfield shows that, while the Met has made some important improvements, nowhere near enough has been done. I agree. Fairfield’s report concludes that the Met remains institutionally racist, sexist and homophobic. This will be acutely concerning for communities across the capital. So, too, will evidence of the Met’s failure to treat many victims of crime with care and compassion at the very moments they need it most. Sadiq Khan is the mayor of London Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in our letters section, please click here . Continue reading...

articles.title: AI's shock-and-awe raid on maths looks like pride before a fall | Rafael Behr
articles.description: Machines are bulldozing through hard problems to assert the power of their tech bro creators, not to advance human knowledge In most walks of life, trying something 12,363,153,437,138 times and getting the same result is reason enough to assume it works every time. Not in maths, where a conjecture that holds up more than 12tn times looks very probably true but doesn’t qualify as proven. That was the status of the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most famous mathematical conundrums in existence, until last week . Then Levent Alpöge, a mathematician working at Anthropic, said he and his collaborator, Claude AI, had crossed the line from conjecture to proof. Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist Continue reading...

articles.title: We’re in a flaking epidemic. No wonder no one wants to host gatherings | Chelsea Flagan
articles.description: We point to self-care as we skip out on activities – but routinely staying home poses its own risk to our mental health You might have heard by now, but Americans are quite lonely , especially if they’re young. The kind of low-effort, high-frequency hanging out we used to rely on – dropping by for dinner, meeting up at the park, watching each other’s kids – has all but evaporated from our lives, leaving us unmoored from the social fabric that underpins our most basic wellbeing. (For reference, chronic loneliness has a comparable impact on long-term health to smoking .) Continue reading...

articles.title: Our ‘Paris manifesto’ proposes how to deal with extreme wealth in the AI age | Open letter
articles.description: It is possible for democracy to reverse the dynamic of oligarchy. But we must act now The explosion of extreme wealth in the world is the defining social fact of our times. When Forbes magazine began ranking the world’s largest fortunes in 1987, the wealth of the richest 0.0001% of our planet’s population equaled 3% of global GDP. Since that time, the wealth held by this tiny group of people – just 3,000 households – has ballooned and now reaches 17% of global GDP. Continue reading...

articles.title: Toddlers are not just little people. Their culture deserves respect | Arwa Mahdawi
articles.description: Small children do not appreciate it when you join in with their singing or throw away their pee-covered leaves. And only a brute would suggest one of them might be tired Nobody can be good at everything, can they? Take me, for example. While I excel at remembering useless facts, going down online rabbit holes and getting toothpaste on my shirt, my singing is so bad it makes small children cry. This is not hyperbole: my five-year-old has wailed on many occasions throughout her short life because I’ve had the temerity to sing along to various TV show jingles or songs. As it turns out, however, it may not just be the fact that I can’t hold a tune that’s upsetting her. I’m not saying that everything I know about parenting I learned from viral posts on the internet, but there was an illuminating tweet doing the rounds last week that said: “Today I learned if you try to sing along with a toddler when you have not been invited to do so, it is a sign of great disrespect in their culture.” I immediately went down an online rabbit hole and discovered various other people have made similar jokes . It’s a common issue. Continue reading...

articles.title: What do Brexit and an Australian cricket scandal have in common? Sometimes it’s right to reopen old wounds | Jonathan Liew
articles.description: Just like the ball-tampering scandal of 2018, the Brexit debate is back. The lesson here is that anything with a dodgy whiff about it will only come back Just move on. You lost, get on with it. Why rake up the past? And why, for the love of all that is holy, is Theresa May back on my television? Of all the many regrettable political figures to have surfaced over recent days, perhaps May has been most triggering of all: a bleak reminder of unhappier times. But of course she has been far from the only former prime minister lured from obscurity by the irresistible siren call of Brexit Revisited. David Cameron has been portending a “very long and painful argument”. “Divisive” and “all-consuming”, argued Rishi Sunak. Boris Johnson warned Andy Burnham – with no apparent sense of irony – that reopening the Brexit negotiations would be “wasting his premiership”. Here they come, the cast of the Tory remake of Avengers: Doomsday, presaging of rancour and paralysis from the people who brought us years of rancour and paralysis. Jonathan Liew is a sportswriter and Opinion columnist for the Guardian The Guardian’s year in review 2026 On Tuesday 1 December 2026, join Guardian writers Zoe Williams

articles.title: Usman Khawaja reveals peace deal text sent to Cricket Australia CEO over sandpapergate
articles.description: CA urged to acknowledge team as a whole knew about ball tampering Khawaja ‘disappointed’ by Pat Cummins’ press conference Usman Khawaja has outlined a proposed joint statement by the entire Australia team of 2018 that would see them accept collective responsibility for ball tampering in South Africa and help them move on from the sandpaper crisis. Speaking to the Grade Cricketer podcast on Wednesday , the former Test opener shared his suggested wording for this collective mea culpa and said it has been put to Todd Greenberg, the chief executive of Cricket Australia, for his consideration. Continue reading...

articles.title: Twickenham confident pitch can take six games in three days for Nations Championship
articles.description: Groundsman on 15-hour days across finals weekend England in home dressing room against All Blacks The Rugby Football Union’s head groundsman is confident Twickenham’s pitch will hold up to staging six matches across three days for the Nations Championship finals, detailing the lengths to which he and his support staff will go. In preparation for the showpiece weekend, the turf – which had been in place since 2012 – was ripped up over the summer with a new state-of-the-art hybrid surface laid. It comes complete with a reservoir that can hold 1.4m litres of water below it – which can be reused using nanobubble technology – and was grown in Scunthorpe before being transported to south-west London. Continue reading...

articles.title: Will Hajime Moriyasu get a high-profile job in Europe after his eight years in charge of Japan?
articles.description: The coach will leave early after the postponement of the Asian Cup and, while there has been clear progress, some had hoped for better results at World Cups A popular Christmas tradition in Japan is to head to KFC but there is an unexpected item on the menu to chew over this year for the millions who do so – a meaty debate over Hajime Moriyasu’s eight years as national-team head coach. Among the many consequences of the Asian Cup’s postponement from January 2027 to December is the fact his tenure has ended early. The 58-year-old was supposed to stay on until February to cap that lengthy spell with (hopefully) a deserved trophy, hand over to Go Oiwa and then, perhaps, blaze a trail to Europe. Instead he left this month, after 113 games in charge during which Japan became a global force to be reckoned with, even if there are those who think he underdelivered. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘It threw me off my bowling a bit’: Isobel Goodwin living dream after England callup
articles.description: London City striker, who was playing tenpin bowling when Wiegman called, says her journey has not been easy Not many phone calls are important enough to justify Isobel Goodwin missing her turn in a game of tenpin bowling. The England head coach ringing to give her a first senior international call-up qualified as an exception for the overjoyed London City Lionesses striker. After scoring with a pin-point finish at the Emirates this month under the gaze of Sarina Wiegman, Goodwin had been hotly tipped to be given a chance with the Lionesses and she is now eager to impress as the squad prepare to face Ukraine in their World Cup qualifying playoff. Continue reading...

articles.title: Florian Wirtz hails Iraola and Klopp as he reaches new levels for Liverpool
articles.description: Playmaker in best form since moving to Anfield ‘I am really enjoying playing under Iraola’ Florian Wirtz has credited Andoni Iraola with helping him recapture the form that made him one of the most coveted players in Europe when he joined Liverpool in a deal worth up to £116m in 2025. The Germany international believes he is in the best form of his Liverpool career, having had a difficult debut season under Arne Slot and also struggled in the early weeks of Iraola’s reign. Wirtz scored an exquisite improvised goal in the 4-0 defeat of Manchester United on Sunday when he also created 10 chances from open play. Continue reading...

articles.title: Has a footballer had a longer career hiatus than Ronaldinho’s 11 year-gap? | The Knowledge
articles.description: Plus: the quickest team to go from FA Cup winners to the first round and matches delayed by snowball fights Mail us with all of your questions and answers “Ronaldinho played for Ravenna, in Serie C, earlier this month. It was his first professional appearance in more than 11 years,” writes George Jones. “Have any other footballers had long career hiatuses? And has any player had a longer hiatus than 11 years?” Ronaldinho’s last professional appearance before his return for Ravenna came on 26 September 2015 for Fluminense, who won 2-0 at home against Goiás. He was withdrawn after 45 minutes. Fans of symmetry will be pleased to see that 11 years and 50 days later, the Brazilian returned for Ravenna in a 2-0 home win against another team with five letters and an accent in their name, Forlì, and was withdrawn after 45 minutes. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘It’s stressful but better than having a proper job’: the life of a cricket umpire
articles.description: Four umpires discuss how they deal with players, why they avoid social media, how technology is changing cricket and why umpiring beats being a football referee By Wisden Cricket Monthly Last summer, sat in a quiet ground at the fag-end of a four-dayer, with a few souls still kicking around and a clutch of cameras streaming what was left of the day live on YouTube, it struck me again what a great, strange sanctuary this place is, out there on the edges of the modern world. The game is trying to move, albeit at its own pace. Later that night, the day’s highlights would be landing on social media, available to all, for the game’s devotees to pore over and pick apart. More people are watching the County Championship than ever before. Streaming numbers show a growing audience in the UK and a widening uptake across the cricketing globe. The numbers aren’t yet earth-shattering, but how could they be, with such eccentric fare? Continue reading...

articles.title: Indian Cockroach movement leader asks court for permission to fly to UK
articles.description: Officials at Delhi airport stopped Saurav Das from boarding flight to Britain, where students have invited him to speak A leader of India’s youth-led Cockroach movement has asked the Delhi high court to give him permission to fly to the UK after immigration officials at Delhi airport stopped him boarding a flight early on Tuesday morning. The court is scheduled to hear Saurav Das’s case on Thursday morning. His lawyer asked the court for a quick hearing because Das has by now already missed some of his engagements at British universities and can only attend the other events on his itinerary if he is allowed to fly out as soon as possible. Continue reading...

articles.title: Trump says pardon for Nvidia boss Huang ‘always an option’ after accusations of breaking export laws – US politics live
articles.description: The US president urged the tech leader to ‘tell the truth’ in upcoming testimony in a Senate hearing Sign up for the Breaking News US email to get newsletter alerts in your inbox ⁠Nine additional ⁠children have ⁠been reunited ​with their ⁠families amid ⁠the ​war ‌in ‌Ukraine, bringing the ‌total to 43 amid an ‌effort led by ​US first lady Melania ⁠Trump, the ​White House ​said. “Children in this region of the world, like children everywhere, cannot possibly understand why geography and government have put them into the horrors of war,” the first lady said in a statement shared first with the Associated Press. Continue reading...

articles.title: Hillsborough law ‘could leave families without vital legal funding after a death’
articles.description: Campaigners say current draft of public office bill would deny bereaved families early access to representation The current draft of the Hillsborough law will leave families without funding in the early stages following a death when legal advice and support are critical, ministers have been warned. The public office (accountability) bill, for which families of victims of the Hillsborough disaster have long campaigned, puts a duty of candour on public officials and is intended to address the inequality of arms between bereaved people and the public bodies from whom they are seeking answers. Continue reading...

articles.title: Midterm gains by US gun control activists’ signals decline of gun lobby
articles.description: More than 200 people endorsed by Everytown for Gun Safety won state and federal races in loss of dominance for NRA The US midterm elections were not only a big win for the Democrats, but also a huge victory for the gun violence prevention movement, and a sign of the declining power of the once-feared gun lobby. More than 200 people who were endorsed by Everytown for Gun Safety, the prominent umbrella organization for a network of violence prevention groups, won state and federal races, according to data the non-profit shared with the Guardian. And nearly 550 former volunteers for Moms Demand Action, a group that is part of the Everytown network, ran for office as incumbents and first-time candidates. Continue reading...

articles.title: Bill McKibben: 2027 may be the year Americans turn on fossil fuels – Stateside with Kai and Carter
articles.description: It’s been another year in which the climate emergency has encroached on the lives of Americans across the country. From gigantic waves battering the California coastline to heat domes driving triple-digit temperatures in the southwest, we are reminded regularly that a crisis is here. Meanwhile, leaders gathered in Turkey for Cop31 failed to reach an agreement on how to move forward, and the US didn’t even bother to show up. To understand this moment, Kai Wright speaks to the environmentalist and author Bill McKibben about what he thinks must be done to slow the rapid advances of global heating, and what he wants to see from Democrats in 2027. Plus, he answers your questions about solar power, and how to talk to your family about the climate emergency Continue reading...

articles.title: Dolphins with active social lives and big friendship groups live longer, Australian researchers discover
articles.description: Decades of data collected at WA’s Shark Bay shows level of socialising may affect longevity for Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphins Dolphins who spend time socialising in large and consistently sized social groups tend to live longer, new research has found. Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphins are marine mammals that can live for more than 50 years and have complex social lives. They spend time socialising in groups – which increase in size during their youth and early adulthood, before declining towards the end of their life, according to a study in PLOS Biology. Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletter Continue reading...

articles.title: M&G boss urges UK to stem flood of firms leaving London Stock Exchange after Compass exit
articles.description: Warning comes after £46bn school and NHS caterer decides to moves main listing to New York, the latest in a long line of departures Business live – latest updates The boss of the British investment group M&G has called on the government to “take a stand” against the long line of companies leaving the London Stock Exchange, after the FTSE 100 caterer Compass announced plans to switch its primary listing to New York. Andrea Rossi, chief executive of M&G, said his fund managers would vote against the Compass’s proposed move. Continue reading...

articles.title: UK embassy in Japan warns of rise in drink spiking and credit card fraud at Tokyo bars
articles.description: Social media campaign fronted by British rapper Shao Dow advises tourists not to let their guard down The British embassy in Tokyo has launched a social media campaign warning visitors to exercise caution after a rise in cases of drink-spiking and credit card fraud against tourists in the Japanese capital. In a recent clip made in conjunction with the embassy, the British rapper and manga artist Shao Dow, a frequent visitor to Japan, notes that although the country “is incredibly safe, that doesn’t mean you can let your guard down”. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘The only free thing is a bed’: hospital patients forced to pay as Malawi runs out of medicines
articles.description: Poor rural families forced to find basic medical supplies as scarcity of foreign exchange paralyses healthcare provision Two days into her stay at Salima district hospital, Maureen Msukwa is still waiting for a painkiller that the hospital pharmacy cannot provide. In the shade of the acacia trees outside the brick maternity block, dozens of relatives sit on woven mats among plastic buckets, cooking pots and basins of laundry. Inside, Msukwa, 25, a pregnant mother from Kasache village in central Malawi, clutches a handwritten scrap of paper instructing her to buy paracetamol from a private vendor across the road. Continue reading...

articles.title: All hostages rescued after Colombian security forces storm supermarket, says president
articles.description: Operation in which one hostage-taker was killed ends daylong siege in Cartagena shopping centre, where 30 people were initially held Colombian security forces have stormed a supermarket in the Caribbean city of Cartagena, ending a daylong hostage siege, with the president saying all those held had been rescued and one hostage-taker killed. Several explosions were heard before security forces entered the building, where about 20 people were believed to be being held by armed men . Continue reading...

articles.title: Iowa town shelters in place as army prepares to detonate entire US stockpile of lead azide
articles.description: Controlled blast to proceed after multiple delays and outpouring of concern about potential health and environmental effects The US Army is set to detonate the nation’s entire stockpile of lead azide in Iowa on Wednesday morning, moving ahead after multiple delays and despite an outpouring of public concern about potential health and environmental effects. The controlled blast is planned to dispose of 9,700lb (4,400kg) of the bomb-making chemicals stored at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, a small town in south-eastern Iowa that is home to about 400 people. The explosion risks releasing plumes of toxic chemicals in a 100-mile (160km) radius, but exactly where those toxins will land has changed as the weather forecast changes. Continue reading...

articles.title: EasyJet boss unable to rule out further job losses after profits collapse by 96%
articles.description: Kenton Jarvis says rival airlines could go bust after Iran war drives sharp rises in fuel prices and hits travel demand Business live – latest updates The boss of easyJet has said he cannot rule out further job cuts and predicted some rival airlines could go bust, after soaring fuel prices this year triggered a collapse in profits. EastJet’s pre-tax profit dropped 96% to £24m in its financial year ending in September, compared with £658m in the previous 12 months. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘It’s been really a mess’: Meta insiders concerned over push to AI content moderation
articles.description: Several employees say rapid speed at which algorithms work means mistakes can happen at greater scale Meta employees have expressed concern at the company’s push to replace human moderators with artificial intelligence, claiming the technology is leading to mistakes with the potential for sweeping political consequences. The social media company, which owns Facebook and Instagram, has been experimenting with AI-driven moderation for years, first introducing it in 2017 to filter out violent extremist content. Continue reading...

articles.title: China-linked battery projects could receive UK funding despite security warnings
articles.description: China-made lithium-ion batteries, which are relatively low-cost, dominate Ofgem project shortlist A string of battery projects linked to China are expected to be granted UK state subsidies despite deepening fears over the risk of foreign interference they could pose to Europe’s energy systems. Ofgem, Great Britain’s energy regulator, published a provisional shortlist for a new “long duration” energy storage scheme in June. The list was dominated by projects relying on lithium-ion batteries, which are typically manufactured in China and operated with Chinese software. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘I had to reject a lot of shame’: Michaela Yearwood-Dan on queerness, Catholicism and her extravagant artist dinner parties
articles.description: The artist adorns her luscious paintings with diaristic notes and confessions. Ahead of an exuberant new show she discusses their unique creation method – and the hunt for her missing cat The artist Michaela Yearwood-Dan is on the hunt for her missing cat. Pinto disappeared from her home in east London a couple of weeks ago and has so far defied the forecasts of tarot readings and the “witchy ladies” predicting his return. A lost pet is not the only thing she’s searching for. “I’m at a stage of life where I’m looking for answers” she says on the eve of her exhibition The Practice of Liberation, at Towner Eastbourne. Her other, more existential questions are those of many women in their early 30s: “Do I want to have children? How do I want to have children? What does my future look like?” She is “big into astrology”, but recently her thoughts have turned to her Catholic upbringing in south London, which serves as a large theme of her exhibition, which debuted at the Whitworth Gallery in Manchester earlier this year. Religious ritual has always appealed to her, and her show uses paintings, ceramics and a musical composition by her friend and longstanding collaborator Alex Gruz to evo

articles.title: ‘I needed to purge it out of me’: the shocking true story behind harrowing drama Josephine
articles.description: Writer-director Beth de Araújo witnessed a brutal sexual assault as a child and has turned her experience into one of the year’s most powerful movies The film-maker Beth de Araújo likens the personal experience that inspired Josephine, her disquieting second feature, to a slow-acting poison. Early one Saturday morning when she was eight years old, Araújo and her father were playing soccer in Golden Gate Park, near their home in San Francisco, when they heard a woman scream. Her father, a former Olympic runner for Brazil, told her to stay and bolted to help; Araújo, scared and alone, ran after him, and instead found the woman in a clearing, naked from the waist down. Araújo was too young to understand what had happened, but she knew something was wrong. So, too, does an eight-year-old Josephine, played by the remarkable newcomer Mason Reeves, in the one scene crafted exactly to Araújo’s memory: Josephine, confused and restless, observes as the woman tucks her hands under her legs to keep them from shaking. She is further confused when her father, Damien, played by the aspirationally everyman actor Channing Tatum, seems extra keen to return to their soccer game afterwards, one of man

articles.title: TV tonight: a gripping psychological thriller that keeps you guessing
articles.description: The revelation of unsavoury secrets throws suspicion on all in Hunting Alice Bell. Plus: sparks fly in First Dates. Here’s what to watch this evening 9pm, Channel 4 The more unsavoury secrets that emerge about each member of the Not Alice Bell group, the harder it is for each of them to avoid suspicion. When Graham Hunter (Ralf Little) escalates his campaign against them, cracks start to appear. Ahead of Thursday’s finale, this mystery is doing a credible job of keeping us guessing. Phil Harrison Continue reading...

articles.title: The Slightest Touch review – running marathons in Colin Farrell and Emma Fogarty’s odd-couple friendship
articles.description: The pair, who met in 2010, are shown preparing for the Dublin race to raise awareness of Fogarty’s epidermolysis bullosa in Rachel Fleit’s considerate documentary The personal scenes in this film from Rachel Fleit have been carefully controlled and curated, the privacy of both parties being important, for different and understandable reasons. But it is an unexpectedly intimate, emotional piece of work, a big-hearted odd-couple story, which is perhaps slightly more complex than at first appears. Emma Fogarty is a smart, garrulous woman from Abbeyleix in County Laois in the Republic of Ireland who has EB: epidermolysis bullosa, a rare condition which means that her skin is permanently, agonisingly painful and requires a daily calvary of bandaging and re-bandaging. While getting an award at the People of the year event in 2010 for her campaigning work educating the public about this illness, Emma met and struck up a friendship with Colin Farrell, a supporter and patron of the EB charity Debra Ireland . Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Working with Kanye West? Talk about intractable egos!’ Caroline Shaw: the Pulitzer-winning composer everyone wants to work with
articles.description: She has collaborated with classical giants such as Anne Sofie von Otter – and pop stars including Phoebe Bridgers. But what happened when Caroline Shaw hit ‘peak hamster wheel’? ‘Look at those!” gasps Caroline Shaw, standing next to me at an old steelworks in Germany’s industrial heartlands. Behind us are defunct concrete cooling towers and, in front, main buildings that sprawl off in a mix of brick and corrugated iron. But Shaw is looking upwards, awed by massive exhaust pipes looming overhead. This place, in the city of Bochum in western Germany, oozes post-industrial chic. These days it’s the Jahrhunderthalle , an arts venue where Shaw is performing later with the Attacca Quartet. For now the complex is shut, so we chat on a concrete bench. Intercepting Shaw, the youngest ever winner of the Pulitzer prize for music, is no mean feat: “in demand” is an understatement for this Portland-based US composer, singer, producer, violinist and viola player. Thirteen years since winning the coveted Pulitzer for Partita for 8 Voices – an exhilarating unaccompanied vocal work that mixes speech and singing, baroque dances and analogue versions of studio-mixed effects – Shaw has a CV like no ot

articles.title: Vaim Hotel by Jon Fosse review – not your typical ghost story
articles.description: The Norwegian Nobel laureate’s sequel to Vaim explores what happens when a man is stripped of everything that tells him who he is Very strange things happen in Jon Fosse’s 2025 novel Vaim . A man meets a woman he secretly loved in his youth while running an errand in a nearby town. She asks him to take her away with him, to the place where they both grew up, on the boat he named after her. She wants to live with him, she tells him, even though she is married, and he has never admitted his feelings. This same man, in another section, has now died. The woman returns to her husband, and tells him he must get back with her, but he has to answer to the name she gave him when they lived together. He must also move into the home of the man she had left him for. “All was strange,” the husband admits, and decides those words should be on his tombstone. Indeed, all is – and remains – very strange to the reader: the powerlessness of these men before this woman they hardly seem to know; the randomness of the events in their lives; their spooky, dream-like surreality. But most of all: Fosse’s narrative choices that thwart easy rationalisation. Vaim Hotel is the second volume in the Nobel laurea

articles.title: Post your questions for Danny Boyle
articles.description: The Trainspotting, Slumdog Millionaire and 28 Days Later director is preparing to launch his biopic of Rupert Murdoch’s early years as a British tabloid mogul. In anticipation of its New Year release, the director will be taking your questions You name it, Danny Boyle has probably directed a movie about it. He’s done zombies in 28 Days Later, astronauts hurtling towards the sun in Sunshine, a man trapped under a boulder in 127 Hours, a world without the Beatles in Yesterday and junkies in Trainspotting. Boyle was born in Radcliffe near Manchester in 1956, and was heading towards the priesthood until, aged 14, a priest of all people talked him out of it. Instead he went into theatre, became deputy director of the Royal Court, then swerved into television, directing Inspector Morse among other things. His first film, Shallow Grave, arrived in 1994; two years later Trainspotting tore British cinema a new one. In 2009, Slumdog Millionaire won him the best director Oscar. He also masterminded the London 2012 Olympics opening ceremony, somehow squeezing industrial chimneys, NHS beds, James Bond, Mr Bean and the history of British pop into one stadium. Continue reading...

articles.title: Tidal bans 100% AI-generated music with plans to delete more than 27m tracks
articles.description: Streaming service says 43% of uploads to platform in past 90 days were made entirely by artificial intelligence The music streaming service Tidal has announced it will ban entirely AI-generated music from its platform and remove millions of songs, saying AI music “diverts streams and royalties away from the artists, and confuses fans”. “To ensure Tidal remains the best place for artists to share their work, and for listeners to enjoy it, we’re removing all tracks that we determine are 100% AI generated,” the company announced on Tuesday. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘As much joy as I could find’: a splash of colour – in pictures
articles.description: From bright green kebab shops to a flash of red stocking, photographer Niall McDiarmid is constantly on the hunt for antidotes to our muted beige and monochrome world Continue reading...

articles.title: Post your questions for Carl Cox
articles.description: Ahead of him rounding out the year at a huge London show, the DJ legend will join us to answer your questions Beatifically smiling as he sends another packed dancefloor into raptures, Carl Cox is one of the most enduring and reliably euphoria-inducing figures in UK club culture history. As he prepares to close out the current season at Drumsheds, the UK’s biggest nightclub, and looks towards a return of his residency at Ibiza nightclub Unvrs, he will join us to answer your questions. Known for playing a banging yet nuanced blend of house and techno, Cox’s career stretches back to the age of 10, learning his craft growing up in London and later Brighton, funding nights out by trimming his neighbours’ hedges. As Chicago house, Detroit techno and other new styles hit the UK, Cox was primed to receive them: fluidly mixing across three decks at once, he immersed himself in both the illegal rave scene and the new wave of nightclubs cropping up to showcase this music. Continue reading...

articles.title: Want to shop more sustainably this Black Friday? The best UK deals on eco-friendly products we love
articles.description: Save money and help the planet with these genuine discounts on everything from bamboo toilet paper to B Corp-certified bedding • The best Black Friday deals • The best Black Friday deals at independent retailers Ethical and sustainable probably aren’t the first words that spring to mind when you think of Black Friday. The annual price-slashing jamboree sits cunningly in wait for your final payday before Christmas, hoping that the dangled carrot of a few quid off will make you more likely to overconsume and overspend. Approach it with care, though, and Black Friday is a good opportunity to buy eco-friendly products that might normally stretch your budget. Many of our Filter recommendations tick either the green box or the affordable box, but we (and you, I expect) would be a lot happier if more of them ticked both. Continue reading...

articles.title: A moment that changed me: at 31 I felt I was running out of time – then my 83-year-old grandma got a tattoo
articles.description: With my career stalled and my dreams unfulfilled, I was starting to write myself off. But my ideas about ageing were all wrong … It was the night before my wedding, in the summer of 2024, and I was a couple of months shy of 31. My bridesmaids and I were having drinks with the North American side of my family before the chaos of the big day. In the two years since I’d last seen my grandma Caroline, who lives in Texas and whom I’ve always called Memom, I’d collected a few new tattoos – and I was worried about showing them to her for the first time as her approval means a lot to me. When Memom saw me, she grabbed my tattooed arm and said: “Let me see.” For a second, I thought she was angry. But to my surprise, she loved them. “These are art!” she said. “Tell me all about them.” I talked her through the abstract fine line piece wrapping around my forearm, and why I’d opted for a filigree dagger in the middle of my upper arm, as well as the significance of the ornamental heart on the back of my right arm. Continue reading...

articles.title: Why I love Budapest in winter: ‘Gloomy days call for a plunge in one of the city’s ornate bathhouses’
articles.description: A neighbourhood that transforms into a living advent calendar, hot chocolate beneath chandeliers and 16th-century baths – Hungary’s capital is full of winter warmth Each December, my neighbourhood on the Buda side of the Danube transforms into a living advent calendar. On the edge of District XI (Újbuda), the 1930s OTI estate in Albertfalva is known for its rustic looking single-storey houses with rounded doorways and green shutters. From 1 December, my neighbours take turns decorating their windows with that day’s number and festive lights, sometimes serving chocolate, cocoa or mulled wine in their front gardens. For something grander, I’ll cross the Danube into Pest for its Christmas markets and elaborately decorated shop fronts. Last November, my friends and I sipped hot chocolate beneath the crystal chandeliers of the Művész Kávéház , a historic cafe on Andrássy út, waiting for the Christmas lights to be switched on outside, illuminating the boulevard and the Hungarian State Opera House. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Sardines are the new anchovies’: what’s hot and what’s not on our winter culinary thermometer
articles.description: Swap your kitchen island for a disco ball and ditch the dill, because blood sausages and burnt honey are in … Salt bread The Korean bakery icon, also known as sogeum-ppang , is made by wrapping pillow-soft bread dough around a baton of cold salted butter, to create a golden-crisp bottom and airy-tender inside as it bakes. Try at Tokkia in Covent Garden and Salted Boy in Paris. Continue reading...

articles.title: Christmas means chocolate – here are my top picks
articles.description: Whether you want the comfort of a traditional festive wreath or something much more startling (I’m talking goat’s cheese and sweet potato jam), I’ve got you covered This time of year is complex. A combination of sadness, joy, loss and acquisition. Winter leaves shed and transform into apricot-gold carpets; we don layers against the cold and the dark; and we wait for Christmas, and a slide into its tinselly, twinkly embrace. articles.title: Sali Hughes on beauty: lactonic scents will have you smelling like cream soda – in a good way
articles.description: These fragrances are on trend right now, and smelling creamy can, it turns out, be surprisingly pleasant When the fragrance world picks a theme, it goes in hard. In the space of one month, I had close to a dozen new “lactonic” (that is, milky or creamy themed) perfumes to try. Instinctively, I wasn’t keen – I haven’t touched a glass of milk since nursery school – and so I eased myself in with DedCool’s Mocha Magic (£24 for 15ml), which adds a shot of coffee to the brand’s Xtra Milk fragrance that I love. This is immediately creamy, rich and bittersweet, like tiramisu, right down to that same dry hit of cocoa powder at the back of the throat. As in life, the coffee wears off, but the vanilla, spice and woody notes hang around for an impressively long spell. As with almost everything right now, it’s sweet, but not overbearingly so. Phlur, so beloved by gen Z, has leapt onboard the trend with Heavy Cream (from £26), available in fragrance and scented body spray. This is creamy, obviously, but also very sweet and immediately brings to mind Swizzels Drumstick lollies and the retro fizzy drink American cream soda. articles.title: NI Water Works - Cornagrade Road Enniskillen 3 Aug
articles.description: Essential Water Infrastructure Improvement Work gets underway – Cornagrade Road, Enniskillen NI Water is set to commence an upgrade of the water infrastructure on Cornagrade Road, Enniskillen in early August for approximately 6 weeks. The work will see around 400m of new watermain being laid along Cornagrade Road, starting at Cherrymount Roundabout on Monday 3 rd August and progressing as far as the second entrance to Kilmacormick Road. To facilitate the laying of this new watermain, a lane closure will be in place around each working area and signage will be in place. Working areas will be kept as short as possible (around 100m) with temporary traffic lights in place to manage the flow of traffic. Access to residential and business properties on and adjacent to Cornagrade Road will be available at all times, although parking spaces within the working area will be affected for a short period of time while the pipelaying passes. Any bus stop located within a working area will be temporarily relocated.

articles.title: Derry - NIW Scheme - Racecourse Rd - from 27 July
articles.description: Essential water network upgrade to get underway on Racecourse Road, Ballyarnett NI Water is set to begin an essential watermain upgrade on Racecourse Road, Ballyarnett (Derry/Londonderry) on Monday 27 th July to improve the resilience of the local water supply network. The work, which involves laying around 170 metres of new watermain between Carnhill Roundabout and Greenhaw Road, will replace a section of the 50-year-old Ballyarnett Water Trunkmain which has been prone to bursts. The upgrade will help to protect homes from flooding, should a burst occur in the future, and provide improved access for NI Water maintenance. A l ane closure controlled by temporary traffic lights will be in place on Racecourse Road around the working area from Monday 27 th July for four weeks. A further two weeks of work will take place in the adjacent verge which will not require any traffic management. Temporary traffic lights will be manned during peak hours and access to properties will be maintained at all times, although parking spaces within the working area will be temporarily unavailable. articles.title: Craigavon - Closure of Maple Path & Parkmore Footbridges
articles.description: Closure of Maple Path and Parkmore Footbridges, Craigavon The Department for Infrastructure have announced that the Maple Path and Parkmore footbridges in Craigavon will be closed from Thursday 4 June 2026. Detailed engineering inspections identified structural concerns, and it has been concluded that the closure of these footbridges is necessary while a permanent solution is developed. Alternative local walking routes are available and will be signposted where appropriate. While these routes may increase journey times for some users, they will provide access around the affected areas. The Department recognises the importance of both footbridges to local residents and apologises for any inconvenience caused. However, as the Department’s infrastructure assets age there will always be an eventual need to replace structures that present safety issues or have come to the end of their natural lifespan. Further information on future proposals for the bridges will be provided as work progresses. The Department would like to thank the public for their patience and cooperation.

Trump issued the order in February 2025, allowing sanctions against those involved in the ICC's efforts to investigate, arrest, or prosecute "a protected person without consent of that person's country of nationality." The president said the court lacks jurisdiction over the United States and Israel. Three of the sanctioned ICC judges - Kimberly Prost, Solomy Balungi Bossa, and Reine Alapini-Gansou - filed a lawsuit in June to challenge the order and the sanctions imposed on them. They accused Trump of exceeding his authority under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) and alleged that their designations for sanctions violated the Administrative Procedure Act. Baghdad wants OPEC+ to recognize a capacity of around 6 million bpd - an important acknowledgment ahead of the group’s upcoming Sunday meeting, at which production targets for 2027 are expected to be a topic of discussion. Under the current OPEC+ production agreement, Iraq's limit is 4.431 million bpd. If OPEC acknowledges the higher capacity assessment that Iraq is requesting, it would give Baghdad a stronger argument for a larger quota. OPEC+ hired outside consultants to assess members' production capabilities before deciding how much oil each country should be permitted to pump. Granting Iraq a larger allocation would mean either allowing more oil onto the market or reducing the amount other members can produce. articles.description: Pension Goes Full CDO: New York's Giant Retirement Fund Bundles Blue Owl, Blackstone Fund Stakes Into $4BN CFO When you can't get out of private credit, you can always lever it up. articles.title: Ugly 5Y Auction: Foreign Demand Slides Resulting In 13th Consecutive Tail, Record Directs
articles.description: Ugly 5Y Auction: Foreign Demand Slides Resulting In 13th Consecutive Tail, Record Directs If yesterday's 2Y auction was average (if maybe modestly strong), then today's 5Y auction was irredeemably ugly.  Starting at the top, today's sale of $70 billion in 5Y paper priced at a high yield of 4.719%, modestly lower than last month's 4.845%, but above the When Issued 4.716%, resulting in a 0.3bps tail, which was the 13th consecutive tail for the 5Y auction - the longest such stretch on record! The bid to cover wasn't too bad - at 2.37 it was fractionally higher than last month's 2.33, and above the six-auction average of 2.31. However, the internals were a mess: Indirects dropped from 60.1% in October to 54.3% in November, the lowest since peak covid (March 2020). This led to Directs surging from 29.4% to 36.7%, the highest on record while Dealers slumped to 9.0%, just a fraction away from the lowest on record. Overall, this was a very ugly 5Y auction, and while the entire yield curve has tightened today thanks to the rush to safety, we would not be surprised to see the selling in stocks shift away to Treasuries. Tyler Durden Tue, 11/24/2026 - 13:22

articles.title: In a flap: how the butterfly became a symbol of gen Z resilience – and anxiety
articles.description: The delicate insect has become fashion’s favourite motif again – but having represented sexuality in the 90s and the soul in Greco-Roman times, what does it say about youth culture today? • Don’t get Fashion Statement delivered to your inbox? Dressed in a fake fur coat and an azure dress, she enters a Christmas party to the twinkly sounds of All I Want For Christmas Is You. There are beautiful people, presents wrapped with Gucci string and butterflies, which have been associated with the popstar since her 1997 album, Butterfly, but have recently fluttered back to become a symbol of gen Z defiance and girlhood. Carey serves as fairy godmother to the other “pop girlies” who have embraced the emblem, from PinkPantheress to Dua Lipa; Rachel Chinouriri to Marina and the Diamonds. At the Academy Museum gala in October, the singer Janelle Monáe looked as if she might take flight in a Robert Wun couture gown, with wide, yonic wings. articles.title: ‘I don’t blame any woman for being sucked in’: how the wellness industry is cynically exploiting menopause
articles.description: Where women see hot flushes and brain fog, pharmaceutical companies see dollar signs. But are products like lion’s mane mushrooms or even magnets for knickers really helping them? Or is it all just a big capitalist con? ‘Tequila?” says a woman brightly, proffering a pink plastic shot glass. It’s barely 10.30 on a Saturday morning, and my perimenopause wellness journey is not going entirely as expected. We are standing in a neon-lit London conference centre amid the hubbub of Pause Live , billed as the UK’s biggest annual women’s health and menopause event and essentially a consumer fair for those in midlife. All around me, women are sampling free squirts of menthol lotion (supposed to cool hot flushes) and paper thimblefuls of slightly grainy, sweet latte made with powdered Peruvian maca root instead of coffee. The tequila, it turns out, is a gift from the sponsors, with no miracle ingredients beyond alcohol. But stalls offer everything from neck creams to pelvic-floor trainers, mindfulness journals and hairpieces for disguising thinning locks, plus herbal supplements in every conceivable edible form: chocolate truffles, ginger shots, mushroom coffee. ( Fungi are big news in the me

articles.title: Interpol and Bloc Party review – two of 00s indie’s most revered acts go toe-to-toe
articles.description: Utilita Arena Cardiff Kele Okereke has a tough challenge selling Bloc Party’s trite latest album – a far cry from Interpol’s ‘masterpiece’ eighth record, performed here to darkly hypnotic effect Try as one might to resist comparison, the balance of this particular yin and yang has been shifting for some time. Twelve months ago, when Interpol and Bloc Party announced a UK and European co-headline tour, the pairing looked like an even contest: two of 00s indie’s most revered acts, whose landmark debuts remain touchstones of the era. Since then, their fortunes have diverged. As an opening bass drone strafes the room, Bloc Party arrive in Cardiff in superficially fine, if puzzling, form. Their seventh album, Anatomy of a Brief Romance, has been met with diminishing returns, its Snapchat-caption triteness – “Every day is such a vibe”, runs one refrain – and creative inertia doing little to win over listeners. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘My name was poison’: Donny Osmond on fame, failure – and his friend Michael Jackson
articles.description: He was the child star of the Osmonds who become a global celebrity by 14. Then, at 21, his career came crashing down. Here, he reveals how he survived his years in exile – and what happened when Jackson was accused of child abuse For a brief period in the early 1970s, Donny Osmond ruled the world. He was the global teenage heart-throb. Even Michael Jackson trailed behind him. He was 14 when his most famous song, Puppy Love, spent five weeks at No 1 in the UK. My sister had a huge poster of him on her bedroom wall. Then again, everybody’s sister had a poster of him on their bedroom wall. Between 1972 and 1973 he had six Top 5 hits in the UK, three of them No 1s (including The Twelfth of Never and Young Love). He was equally successful back home in the US. Osmond was clean-cut, religious and respectful, with a mighty ability to punch out cover versions of saccharine standards. From his purple velvet cap to his doleful eyes and dazzling all-American smile, he was a marketing dream. We’d only just finished with Beatlemania. And now there was Donnymania. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘What if joining the resistance got your friends executed?’ The chilling new films casting Nazi collaborators in a fresh light
articles.description: For decades, films about Nazi-occupied Europe were all about the fearless resistance while despicable collaborators deserved all they got. So what’s behind the spate of movies portraying turncoats in a more sympathetic light? A young maid busies herself in a vast, high-ceilinged apartment, serving her master steaming coffee in fine china and polishing the hefty family silver, as she picks her way across the checkerboard parquet lit by stylish Poul Henningsen lamps. Woman Unknown , which won the Golden Lion at the Venice film festival this year, is set in the immediate aftermath of Denmark’s liberation from Nazi rule, but you wouldn’t know that from the opening scenes: five years of occupation, martial law and rationing have left the splendour of the Danish bourgeoisie miraculously untouched. The trauma of wartime violence only comes rushing back in occasional bursts: blurry flashbacks show shadowy figures pointing guns at temples and bodies thudding to the floor. But the red fabric billowing through the fog of her memory is not the Nazi flag but liberated Denmark’s white-crossed Dannebrog . The black-clad executioners are not SS officers but resistance fighters reckoning with colla

articles.title: Dapper Liam and Noel, experimental Björk, and Bowie ‘cuddling himself’: Rankin reveals his never-before-seen shots of the stars
articles.description: After some satirical experiments with the ‘disgusting’ AI, the photographer has returned to his first love with a book of contact sheets from his celebrity shoots. ‘I wish we could go back and stop everything changing,’ he says “I hate AI,” says Rankin. “A lot of people think I’m an evangelical twat about it, and I’m not. I think it’s disgusting. I think the people who run it are disgusting. They’ve made a massive gamble with humanity and society and culture.” His contempt may surprise anyone who’s familiar with Rankin’s substantial AI output. Ever since the artist Damien Hirst introduced him to the possibilities of generative AI in 2021, the British photographer has been going further down the rabbit hole. “I’m not somebody who likes to be critical about something without actually knowing about it,” he explains. “I’ve gone deep into trying to work it out.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Is it true that … we only use 10% of our brains?
articles.description: The idea that we access a fraction of our cognitive potential goes back decades, but does medical science agree? This idea really bugs Dr Mary Spiller , senior lecturer in the University of East London’s Department of Psychology and Human Development, who’s shocked by how prevalent it remains, despite being untrue. Spiller says the myth’s origins can partly be traced to the work of William James, one of the founders of modern psychology, working in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. He wrote: “We are making use of only a small part of our possible mental and physical resources.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Will the Jilly Cooper plagiarism allegations taint our love of Rivals? I doubt it | Nadia Khomami
articles.description: The evidence seems overwhelming, but artists and writers have borrowed from each other for hundreds of years. The line between homage and theft is a thin one “Immature poets imitate; mature poets steal,” the poet TS Eliot wrote a century ago. No work of art, he argued, exists in a vacuum. Great writers draw on what came before them, transforming their influences into something entirely their own. Eliot’s words came to mind when I read the revelations about the queen of the country house bonkbuster Jilly Cooper, who has been accused of “extensive and deliberate” plagiarism in her 1978 book Prudence. At least 35 passages appear to have been lifted from The Serial, a satirical novel by American writer Cyra McFadden, alongside remarkable similarities to sections of Josephine Tey’s 1948 novel The Franchise Affair. McFadden’s daughter is threatening legal action, describing the treatment of her mother’s work as “unconscionable”. Nadia Khomami is arts and culture correspondent at the Guardian Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in our letters section, please click h

articles.title: The pet I’ll never forget: Susan Badger, the stray dog saved by a box of fried chicken
articles.description: No one could get close to this odd-looking pup when she appeared at a Maryland construction site. But hunger brought her in from the cold – and gave her a loving home I was driving to a doctor’s appointment in March when I saw a scruffy dog just sitting on the side of the Baltimore-Washington Parkway at a construction site, watching traffic go by. I noticed that she wasn’t wearing a collar. I thought to myself, that dog clearly doesn’t belong there – she needs help. Why is she out on her own? Workers at the construction site had built her a small shack, complete with a water bowl and food dish. Although she was spending some time there, whenever they would get too close she would run off. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Two million people tuned in to see me mash potatoes!’ Gregor Fisher on his remarkable rebirth after Rab C Nesbitt
articles.description: For almost 30 years Fisher played a drunk in a string vest. Now a new generation has come to know him through his cooking videos. He talks about family secrets, cancelled shows and the correct approach to butter Gregor Fisher’s kitchen is so tidy – it looks as if he has just finished cleaning it – that I begin to worry he has forgotten (or was possibly never apprised of) our arrangement. After he makes me a coffee and we sit at the square table, I feel obliged to raise the subject: aren’t we gonna cook something? “I thought we’d do some brunch,” he says. He steps into his larder and returns a moment later with the makings of kedgeree, prepared and covered in clingfilm: chopped onions, minced shallots, hard-boiled eggs, halibut from a fishmonger in Largs. Continue reading...

articles.title: Cookie fever! How does Marks & Spencer knock out so many viral food sensations?
articles.description: Chicken kievs, ‘picky bits’, strawberry and cream sandwiches: the hits have been coming for almost half a century. Now Kathryn Turner, M&S’s head of product development, has become a social media celebrity. What’s the secret ingredient? The scenes in a Liverpool Marks & Spencer , after the release of the chain’s chocolate and cornflake cookie earlier this month, looked like brink-of-Covid panic buying crossed with a zombie apocalypse. It probably didn’t help that the baked goods hit the shelves at around the time the government started asking Britons to plan for an unnamed near-term disaster . How would we cope with a national emergency when we coped this badly with the crisis of not enough biscuits? You could explain the M&S cookie fever with reference to the company’s product development icon, Kathryn Turner, who has half a million followers between Instagram and TikTok, or the powerful urge to belong, in gen Z particularly. But it surely has something to do with the biscuit itself. As Rosie Sykes, the author of The Friday Biscuit, says: “Biscuits are very much part of the national fabric.” But lately they’ve had this “slightly weird glow-up”, gone “a bit max”, Sykes says. Whatev

articles.title: Council tax and stamp duty: both are a disaster zone. Scrap them and start from scratch | Polly Toynbee
articles.description: These ancient and often grossly unfair taxes are stifling the economy and young people. It’s long past time for radical reform When voters were asked in 2020 which tax they would cut first , council tax came out on top, and rightly so. Still, it’s taken six years for an array of Labour and Liberal Democrat MPs to call for reforms to this most grotesquely unjust tax. Prompted by a public petition organised by the campaign Fairer Share, a Westminster Hall debate heard calls for a review into property taxes, which would lay out options for replacing council tax and stamp duty land tax. Labour MPs were among those who have signed a letter to Downing Street calling for property tax reform to be a priority in Andy Burnham’s upcoming 10-year plan . Among flotillas of economists and thinktanks who signed the letter is Lord O’Neill, a Burnham adviser and former Goldman Sachs economist, who calls UK property taxation “utterly nonsensical”. Burnham has frequently backed reform of the “highly regressive” council tax and stamp duty, labelling them as “a tax on the aspiration of young people”. Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist Continue reading...
