Some of their assumptions are questionable, however, and their sums do not factor in what Brexit continues to cost us. The Guardian's Brussels correspondent, Jennifer Rankin, fact-checks the claim Is £750m a week the real cost of rejoining the EU – or the Brexit bus myth all over again? Continue reading...

articles.title: You Can See Everything’s chaotic battle for the narrative about Elizabeth Holmes
articles.description: In Nathan Fielder’s new documentary, the protagonists and film-makers battle over who is the hero and who is the villain. It’s a fascinating insight into modern celebrity promotion • Don’t get the Close Up delivered to your inbox? Sign up here Thank you for signing up to the Close Up newsletter. This is our first-ever edition! And, just like on the show , I’ll be zooming in on the big culture questions and recommending things I’m obsessed with. I’ll also give you a sneak peek of what’s coming up on the show and what the team have been talking about behind the scenes. OK, I’ll admit it: I wanted to hate You Can See Everything, the A24 documentary about Theranos fraudster Elizabeth Holmes, which finally arrived in UK cinemas last week. The marketing was slick, the hype was unparalleled. I didn’t believe a three-hour documentary about a disgraced tech CEO could be that good. But, like our colleague Adrian and basically every film critic who’s seen it, I left the cinema thinking: that was amazing and what on earth did I just watch? Continue reading...

articles.title: Hexed review – Disney’s witchy caper is a wicked disappointment
articles.description: A teen girl discovers she is a witch in this mostly magic-free reminder that original animation is stuck in an unoriginal place As bleak as Disney’s overreliance on sequels might have become, it’s not quite as bleak as the crumbling state of its original output. Obviously because of the former, the latter category has become that much less populated but even when the studio has recently bothered to release something without a number in the title, it’s been hard to really see the point. With or without Pixar, films like Elio, Strange World, Raya and the Last Dragon, Luca, Elemental, Onward and Wish have all felt as uninspired as something a rival might try to desperately cobble together in an attempt to lure kids away from Disney. Three Thanksgivings ago, Wish was a particularly poor yet extremely smug example of how rubbishy things have got, a personality-free princess tale that doubled up as a 100-year anniversary victory lap. It was Disney’s worst-reviewed animated film in almost two decades and its deserved box office failure cost about $131m. Unperturbed, its co-director Fawn Veerasunthorn (along with Moana 2 director Jason Hand) is back this holiday with another rote rip-off a

articles.title: ‘The Terence Conran of his day’: the visionary Victorian futurist adored by design superstars today
articles.description: A professor at the age of 21, Christopher Dresser was a design genius who created beautiful, futuristic homeware, from teapots to toast racks to jugs. Why is his brilliance only now being recognised? Victorian industrial designer Christopher Dresser was always a visionary. As a child, he was so artistically gifted he went to design school in 1847 when he was just 13. He became a professor at 21, dreaming up theories based on plant structure that changed the way designers worked. But it was after he quit academia that he really started to break boundaries. As a self-declared “design doctor”, he experimented with production techniques that brought beautiful, futuristic homeware into everyday houses. He was one of the first western designers to travel to Japan, helping introduce Japonisme to British life, which has had a transformative effect on furniture and decoration ever since. Continue reading...

articles.title: Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia is elite impunity | Moira Donegan
articles.description: After the CEO was reinstated after Trump’s pressure campaign, it is abundantly clear: there are different rules for rich people There are different rules for rich people. If you or I acted the way that Jensen Huang has been accused of acting – allegedly berating and mistreating employees, sleeping with subordinates, and seeming to carry on a staggering number of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman identified by US intelligence as a likely Chinese spy who helped smuggle the company’s product to China – we probably would find ourselves out of work and out of favor for quite some time. But this is not so for Huang, the tech founder and close ally to Donald Trump who was recently ousted from Nvidia, the chip manufacturer he founded. On Monday, after a pressure campaign from Donald Trump, JD Vance and other members of the Trump administration, Huang was reinstated as CEO by the Nvidia board. Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnist Continue reading...

articles.title: Mariella Frostrup calls AJ Odudu ‘aggressive’ – and here we go again. We tire of this angry black woman trope | Natalie Morris
articles.description: Microaggressions pile up, and then they are triggering. Amid the latest row on I’m a Celebrity, we’re obliged to explain this hurt all over again When I heard Mariella Frostrup call AJ Odudu “aggressive” over the weekend on I’m a Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here!, my heart sank with sick recognition. For her part, AJ’s mother has since said that watching her daughter experience this all-too-familiar dynamic was a “living hell”. I know many Black women tuning in will have felt a collective shudder of disgust and solidarity. Of course, there is pushback. “Our addiction to offence is tearing us apart,” wrote a Telegraph pundit on Monday . But, this language is not neutral. There is a long history of Black women having their conduct and tone disproportionately scrutinised by white people. And what happened between Odudu and Frostrup is a tale as old as time. A Black woman stands up for herself and, no matter how reasonably she presents her argument, she is accused of aggression. It is an efficient tactic to flip the focus on to the behaviour of the Black woman, and it is rooted in racist stereotypes. Natalie Morris is the author of Mixed/Other: Explorations of Multiraciality in Modern Br

articles.title: Why the genocide verdict against Myanmar has big implications for Israel | Geoffrey Robertson
articles.description: Proving the ‘crime of crimes’ against an individual is notoriously difficult, but the ICJ has set a precedent for states to be found liable. Israel could be next For the first time ever, a state has been found guilty of genocide – that “crime of crimes” – and has been ordered to compensate victims and to prosecute and punish the perpetrators. This judgment came from the international court of justice (ICJ), which has convicted Myanmar of killing and expelling many thousands of Rohingyas in Rakhine state in 2017 . The court did not change the definition of the crime, settled by the genocide convention in 1948 as requiring proof of an intention to destroy, in whole or part, a racial or religious group as such. But it made the prospect of proving this against a nation a good deal easier than against an individual. It set a precedent for its next case concerning state liability, namely the case brought by South Africa against Israel. Geoffrey Robertson KC was a UN appeal judge and is author of World of War Crimes – Eyeless in Gaza and Beyond Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered f

articles.title: Compass’s logic for US listing is flimsy but UK ministers need to wake up to Footsie flight risk | Nils Pratley
articles.description: The contract caterer switching to New York is a big hit to the London Stock Exchange but what is being done to discourage others from delisting? That’s gratitude, eh? Compass Group built its business, in part, on contracts to serve dinners in British schools and run catering operations in NHS hospitals. Now it plans to switch its primary stock market listing to New York in 2028. Compass is a bad one for the London market to lose. First, it is the 18th largest company in the FTSE 100 index and one of the few that is the biggest in the world in its market (contract catering, not just for the public sector but for thousands of corporate clients). Second, its reasons for joining the stateside listing rush feel flimsy – but also dangerous. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Ukraine-Russia war is escalating – and it will go global unless Europe speaks with one voice | Simon Tisdall
articles.description: Attacks from the Mediterranean to eastern Europe to the Baltic Sea are a rebuke to western complacency. Trump is a liability, and he must be bypassed to ensure peace Ukraine’s spectacularly successful weekend drone attack on a spanking new Russian warship docked in the Libyan port city of Benghazi, more than 1,300 miles (2,200km) from Kyiv, is further proof, if it were needed, that the catastrophic full-scale war Vladimir Putin launched in 2022 is escalating and spreading uncontrollably. The sinking follows a similar incident in the Baltic last week, which crippled a Russian cargo ship, and previous Ukrainian attacks on oil tankers and Russian navy ships and bases in the Black Sea region. Last week, Russia was blamed for a missile and drone strike on Nato member Poland , which Donald Tusk, the Polish prime minister, claimed was intentional, and for deliberately targeting western diplomatic compounds in Kyiv. While Moscow’s murderous winter bombing of Ukrainian civilians and energy infrastructure continues apace, provocative and disruptive Russian hybrid warfare operations across all of Europe, including sabotage, arson and cyber-attacks, are becoming daily occurrences. Simon Tisdal

articles.title: Pochettino criticises Premier League officiating after Yoro red card overturned
articles.description: Manchester United defender wrongly sent off in 4-0 loss ‘If we have VAR, what were they doing?’ asks head coach Mauricio Pochettino has criticised officiating in English football, saying: “We have an unbelievable car, but we need to be in the level to drive [it],” after Leny Yoro’s Anfield red card was overturned on Tuesday. Despite the Football Association ruling the Frenchman’s early sending-off in Sunday’s 4-0 defeat at Liverpool was “wrongful dismissal”, Manchester United remain furious at the decision, and at Pro Ref, the elite officials’ organisation. Continue reading...

articles.title: UK nations in dark over whether they will get automatic entry to 2035 Women’s World Cup
articles.description: Fifa will make decision on qualifying procedures Four 2031 hosts have been given automatic places England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales are in the dark about whether they will be granted automatic qualification as hosts for the 2035 Women’s World Cup . The decision on qualification procedures will be made by Fifa, with sources at the domestic football associations telling the Guardian they had yet to be informed of the plan after their bid was formally accepted. Continue reading...

articles.title: Outcry grows over Labour plan to exempt most brownfield sites from nature protection rules
articles.description: Chancellor’s decision to exempt plots up to 1.5 hectares allows developers to dodge rules aiming to reverse wildlife declines An outcry is growing over the UK chancellor’s removal of most brownfield housing plots from a legal requirement for developers to measurably enhance nature. John Healey’s decision in the budget to exempt brownfield plots of up to 1.5 hectares from biodiversity net gain (BNG) laws effectively means housing developers of inner-city, urban and surburban sites will be able to dodge rules designed to reverse steep wildlife declines while also allowing housebuilding growth. According to government data, 86% of brownfield sites currently registered are 1.5ha or under. Continue reading...

articles.title: Trump honors Rudy Giuliani with presidential medal of freedom
articles.description: President’s former lawyer, disbarred over effort to overturn 2020 election result, receives top civilian honor Donald Trump awarded Rudy Giuliani, his former personal attorney who was disbarred for his efforts to help the US president overturn 2020 election results , with the presidential medal of freedom on Tuesday. “I am honored and humbled to receive the Presidential Medal of Freedom from my nation and from President Donald J Trump,” Giuliani, 82, wrote in an X post hours after the award had been presented to him. Continue reading...

articles.title: Summer heat deaths in 2026 reached record high of 5,258 in England
articles.description: Figure for May to September is far higher than previous peak of 2,985 since records began a decade ago More than 5,200 deaths in England in 2026 were linked to summer heat, the highest provisional annual total since records began a decade ago, according to the UK Health Security Agency. The government agency said 5,258 deaths were associated with extreme heat between May and September 2026. Continue reading...

articles.title: Their loss changed Appalachian forests for ever. Now the American chestnut is back
articles.description: The trees have been functionally extinct in the US for nearly a century. But new techniques are creating plants resistant to the parasitic blight that almost wiped them out Jeff White is starstruck by a tree. The farmer and environmentalist from rural Maryland has an affinity with the American chestnut but has never seen one stretch from root to sky like this one. “About how tall is it?” he asks. “Over 70ft [21 metres],” says Cassie Stark, director of science implementation for the American Chestnut Foundation (TACF). “Just incredible,” White says, his gaze fixed upwards. “I’ve never seen one so tall and so healthy.” ‘Thompson’, above left, is an unusually tall specimen of an American chestnut, a now-rare species once ubiquitous in the US. Jeff White next to ‘Gladys’, a thriving 15-metre-tall pure American Chestnut in Virginia’s Lesesne forest Continue reading...

articles.title: NHS caterer Compass confirms plan to ditch main London listing for New York
articles.description: World’s largest catering group supplies big tech firms such as Microsoft, Google and Amazon in the US London’s stock market has been dealt a further blow as the catering company Compass Group confirmed plans to move its main listing to the US , saying it had become “a predominantly North American business”. The world’s largest catering group said the move would provide better access to “the world’s largest and deepest pool of capital,” as it kicked off a consultation with its shareholders, two-fifths of whom are based in the US. Continue reading...

articles.title: BBC’s preschool shows to be made available in CBeebies hub on Netflix
articles.description: Teletubbies, Numberblocks and Hey Duggee among 24 shows to be trialled on world’s biggest streaming service Teletubbies, Numberblocks and Hey Duggee are among a host of the BBC’s preschool shows to be made available on Netflix, as the broadcaster battles to arrest a generational shift away from its programming. In an unprecedented six-month trial, a dedicated CBeebies hub will be set up on the world’s biggest streaming service, with a substantial selection of 24 shows to choose from. It will include some of the BBC’s best-known titles and characters. Continue reading...

articles.title: Meta launches Muse in UK – the AI agent that can do your Christmas shopping
articles.description: Users can give agents tasks such as booking travel or buying presents, but glitches have been reported Have you downloaded Meta’s AI assistant Muse or do you plan to? Want to avoid the Christmas shopping hordes? Then let your AI agent do the shopping for you. Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta is launching its Muse AI assistant in the UK and is encouraging users to let it loose on your apps – and the high street. Muse has been a hit in the US and is ranked first and second respectively on Google and Apple’s free app stores, having been downloaded millions of times. However, UK regulators have said they are keeping a close eye on the launch over privacy and consumer protection requirements. Continue reading...

articles.title: Scream 4 came out 15 years ago – but its mockery of online brainrot is more spot-on than ever
articles.description: When Wes Craven’s final slasher film came out, correctly predicting clout-chasing influencers and social media’s corruption of our lives, Instagram was just six months old Get our weekend culture and lifestyle email It has been almost a year since Australia’s social media ban for under-16s and it seems as though nothing has been able to effectively deter the youth from the slippery slope of internet addiction – even when they have expressed the desire to quit . It’s hard to believe that it has only been a decade since TikTok condemned us to the eternal doomscroll and just over 15 years since Instagram launched. Surely no one predicted just how much the online world would be leeching off of us, right? Well, Wes Craven did. Craven is the mind behind notable horror titles including The Hills Have Eyes, A Nightmare on Elm Street and the Scream franchise – and the last film he directed, four years before his death in 2015, was Scream 4. Continue reading...

articles.title: The World of Love review – beautifully directed and compellingly elusive family mystery
articles.description: Yoon Ga-eun’s film tracks the uneasy fallout after a teenage schoolgirl makes a deeply shocking announcement to her class Korean film-maker Yoon Ga-eun creates a strange world of bewilderment, sadness and pain – but not much of love – in this involving and mysterious family drama. It seems always to be gesturing at an indefinable sense of loss, a poignant keynote struck by the recurring soundtrack piano arrangement of Bach’s Sheep May Safely Graze. Seo Su-bin gives an excellent performance as Joo-in, a high schooler possessed of a cheeky, madcap sense of fun, like her wacky, magic-obsessed kid brother Hae-in (Lee Jae-hee). She is keen on taekwondo and often shown (in borderline-uncomfortable closeup) kissing boyfriends that she will later dump. But when classmate Su-ho (Kim Jeong-sik) asks her to sign a petition objecting to the release and local rehousing of a convicted child rapist, Joo-in refuses, on the ostensible grounds that the petition talks about the permanent damage done to rape victims. Joo-in astonishes and upsets the class by announcing at the top of her voice that she herself is a rape victim, and she has not been permanently damaged – and then says it was just a joke

articles.title: To Hold a Mountain review – a spectacular setting for tough savvy woman’s fight against the government
articles.description: A livestock farmer with a sad secret in her past rallies to keep military training out of her breathtaking mountain home in Montenegro An award-winner in Sundance, where it premiered earlier this year, this slow-burn documentary follows a middle-aged Montenegrin livestock farmer called Gara and her 13-year-old daughter Nada. The two of them eke out a hardscrabble living on Sinjajevina, a breathtaking mountain plateau on which Montenegro’s government would like to conduct training exercises for its own army as well as Nato’s. This goes down about as well as a wolf in the sheep pen with flinty Gara, who rallies her neighbours as well as the local media to fight the proposal. She displays a savviness that’s somewhat surprising, even if her fortitude and strength of conviction seem completely in character. However, that fight against the state is just one element of a film that, through long, languid takes, reveals the women’s stately pastoral existence, one taken up above all with care for their menagerie of animals (cows, sheep, goats, cats and dogs) and each other. Co-directors Petar Glomazić and Biljana Tutorov gradually reveal the family setup isn’t exactly what it appears at firs

articles.title: TV tonight: friends Prue Leith and Sandi Toksvig take a special holiday
articles.description: The TV chef takes her sardonic chum on a tour of her South Africa hometown. Plus: Nigella Lawson gets her teeth into the Bake Off finalists’ showstoppers. Here’s what to watch this evening 9.15pm, Channel 4 Prue Leith was born and brought up partly in Cape Town, and she has always wanted to share South Africa’s beauty with her friend Sandi Toksvig. This pleasant working holiday is the result, and it’s impossible to miss the warmth between the pair. But as they take a cable car up Table Mountain, ponder the horrors of apartheid and enjoy a barbecue, nothing feels particularly revelatory. Phil Harrison Continue reading...

articles.title: The Song of Stork and Dromedary by Anjet Daanje review – don’t miss this glorious epic inspired by Emily Brontë
articles.description: The afterlife of a Yorkshire village girl who becomes a gothic literary icon is explored across three centuries, in a thrilling paean to the power of books I had a plan. I was going to nibble away at this great wedge of a book, a morsel a night, like a little reading mouse. But then the story swallowed me whole. I read Dutch author Anjet Daanje’s The Song of Stork and Dromedary over three feverish nights, and spent the days in between longing for the dark. This 720-page novel should come with a warning label: may cause severe infatuation. We begin in the fictional Yorkshire village of Bridge Fowling with Susan Knowles-Chester, a woman who attends to the dead. The year is 1847, and Susan knows the old ways, the threshold rituals: how to arrange a corpse so it doesn’t gape and gawp at the living. “The villagers have a horror of her work, for wherever she goes, she leaves grief like driftwood in her wake, yet when the time comes, many ask for her help, it is an open secret.” Continue reading...

articles.title: First Children’s Booker prize reveals ‘Great Eight’ shortlist
articles.description: Judge Frank Cottrell-Boyce introduces the eight titles shortlisted for the inaugural £50,000 award, by authors including Shaun Tan, Eoin Colfer and Liz Hyder Books by the Oscar-winning artist Shaun Tan, Artemis Fowl author Eoin Colfer and Nero award-winner Liz Hyder are among the eight titles shortlisted for the first Children’s Booker prize. The award, the Booker prize foundation’s first for children’s fiction, launched last year amid concern that children’s enjoyment of reading had fallen to its lowest level in 20 years . Explore the shortlist for the Children’s Booker prize 2027 and, for a limited time, get all eight books for £80 at guardianbookshop.com . Delivery charges may apply. Continue reading...

articles.title: Kate Bush and Grace Jones urge Australian government not to legalise AI ‘theft’
articles.description: Singers among 7,000 artists and creatives urging Labor to protect copyright law in face of lobbying from AI companies Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Kate Bush, Grace Jones and Sir Ian Rankin have joined 7,000 artists and creatives around the world pleading for the Australian government not to weaken copyright law, urging Labor not to “legalise the theft of the work of the world’s creators on their soil”. The international push, the latest in a global pushback against artificial intelligence companies and their requests to water down copyright, comes the same day a long-awaited parliamentary committee handed down a mammoth report calling for copyright reform in Australia. Continue reading...

articles.description: Robert Nickelsberg has been photographing the plight of the Kashmiri people for more than 20 years – his images reveal how trauma has settled into the fabric of everyday life Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘The food of emperors’: a Chinese restaurant turns boring turkeys into crispy showstoppers
articles.description: Chicago’s Sun Wah BBQ started a new Turkey Day tradition for immigrants and other neighbors: allowing them to bring in their fowl and roast it in the fragrant Hong Kong-style Tell us: do you have a special new year food tradition? Download Feast , with more than 7,000 global recipes from Guardian chefs like Yotam Ottolenghi and Meera Sodha Behind an Uptown Chicago facade of glass and green-glazed bricks, rows of mahogany-red ducks glisten. This neighborhood is sometimes called “New Chinatown”, sometimes “Little Vietnam ”. And this tidy restaurant is Sun Wah BBQ , which Eric and Lynda Cheng opened in 1987. Today, it’s also an unlikely Thanksgiving destination. Continue reading...

articles.title: Crunch time: Niki Segnit’s five rules for winter salads
articles.description: Plus five fantastic recipes, from seared tuna and potato to spicy butternut and lentil, to show how it’s done Approach a winter salad as you would your winter wardrobe – with clever layering. With the greatest respect to Coco Chanel, and her famous rule about taking one item off when you think you’re done, in this instance I favour assembling a salad and then adding an ingredient. Unlike in baking, where departing from a recipe can have its risks, improvisation rewards the salad maker. Still, if you’re planning a winter salad, especially if it’s a main meal, you might want to use a checklist to avoid some common pitfalls. The most egregious of these is cosy dullness. It’s all too easy to throw together some fresh winter produce and end up with a dish that’s more like a cold risotto or yesterday’s traybake. This often comes down to the combination of roasted root vegetables and “interesting” grains. What makes a salad a salad is its invigorating qualities, but root veg and cereals are sweet, with earthy, nutty flavours and soft textures; the pairing might be a modern classic but it’s about as invigorating as a warm bath. Not that you should avoid the combination; you just want to ba

articles.title: Thomasina Miers’ recipe for fried fish with red pipián, and celeriac and leek rice
articles.description: Packed with flavour and natural goodness, spicy Mexican pipián sauce goes brilliantly with white fish, while a garlicky vegetable rice is perfect on the side As the weather closes in, I find my cooking naturally moving towards comfort as well as goodness. I have been ill recently, and while my natural inclination is to cook food that I want to eat, our bodies are clever organisms and, as is often the case, the food we crave is often the food that our systems need. A pipián is rather like a revved-up Mexican korma, with toasted, ground pumpkin seeds adding a deliciously nutty backdrop to charred tomatoes, fruity, mild guajillo chillies and light spices. It is a wonderful thing to eat with fried fish on a cold night. The garlicky, celeriac-studded rice is the perfect accompaniment. Continue reading...

articles.title: How a tiny rare frog became an ecological warning sign for Madagascar
articles.description: The golden mantella is said to be found wherever gold is, making its habitat a target for illegal mining, which is destroying fragile ecosystems across the country As Albert Rakotoarisoa emerges from the forest into a clearing in Mangabe reserve in the east of Madagascar, he sees dozens of holes dug in the marshy ground, a sign that people have been here to search for gold. “I came a couple of weeks ago, and these weren’t here,” he says as he surveys the damage, counting 40 holes. “I’m really disappointed.” Continue reading...

articles.description: The Guardian’s picture editors select photographs from around the world Continue reading...

articles.title: Robert Pattinson is not enough: who should become the new Bond girl?
articles.description: With the British actor securing the role of James Bond, speculation has now begun over who should join him in Denis Villeneuve’s much-anticipated caper After years of speculation, Robert Pattinson has been officially cast as James Bond for a new Amazon-produced film directed by Denis Villeneuve. There’s no release date for the project yet, though fall 2028 seems a likely target, given the release dates of all of the Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig installments. This leaves plenty of time left on the clock for more speculation – namely, about who will be cast as the so-called Bond Girls for this rebooted installment. Past Bonds have usually been recognizable from earlier work, but none of them had yet reached Pattinson’s level of fame before actually playing Bond. Given that, in addition to sterling indie work for directors like David Cronenberg, Claire Denis and Lance Oppenheim, Pattinson has also been in Twilight, Batman and Christopher Nolan movies, he’s arguably already as famous as Brosnan and Craig were at their 007 peak. It must be this shift in the casting status quo that has inspired some predictions or hopes for a quantity as known as, say, Sydney Sweeney to play a Bond gi

articles.title: NHS trusts to be investigated over ‘repeated failures’ to admit treatment errors
articles.description: Failing in their legal duty of candour adds to the distress of patients and families and damages trust, says England’s public service ombudsman Hospitals will be investigated for regularly breaching their legal duty to tell patients and their relatives when mistakes have happened. The public service ombudsman for England is launching an investigation into “repeated failures” by NHS trusts to discharge their “duty of candour” to admit when treatment errors have led to patients dying or suffering harm. Continue reading...

articles.title: Hundreds of thousands could lose disability benefits under Timms plans for Pip shake-up
articles.description: Minister’s review says Pip system no longer fit for purpose and recommends new test for who is allowed to claim Hundreds of thousands of people face losing their disability benefits under plans being considered by ministers as part of a shake-up of the welfare system. Officials are drawing up plans to redesign the personal independence payment (Pip) system for adults in England and Wales after the work and pensions minister, Stephen Timms, deemed it “no longer fit for purpose”. Continue reading...

articles.title: Thomas Markle, father of Meghan, indicted over child sexual abuse material
articles.description: Markle was initially released by a Florida court but later jailed after cutting off his ankle monitor Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex , has been indicted by a federal grand jury in Los Angeles on two counts of possessing child sexual abuse material. Markle, 82, was indicted in federal court on Tuesday, US prosecutors said. Continue reading...

articles.title: Chicken Shop Date host says she ended YouTube show … to find a real date
articles.description: Amelia Dimoldenberg described two panic attacks and said she wanted to end the hit series ‘before I start resenting it’ Amelia Dimoldenberg, the host of Chicken Shop Date, has said she decided to end the popular YouTube series which had increasingly left her feeling “isolated” and made her search for real relationships more challenging. The comedian, 32, also revealed she had questioned the future of the interview series after suffering two panic attacks, saying she wanted to end it “before I start resenting it”. Continue reading...

articles.title: Trump makes millions after pressuring Nvidia to reinstate Huang - The Latest
articles.description: Jensen Huang has been reinstated as CEO of AI chip powerhouse Nvidia, just 11 days after his resignation. The shock decision came after Donald Trump and senior White House officials lobbied the Nvidia board, claiming Huang posed no security risk despite an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. As the chip firm’s share price soared, Guardian columnist and Politics Weekly America host Jonathan Freedland tells Lucy Hough how Trump made millions overnight Continue reading...

articles.title: Prue and Sandi’s South African Adventure review – you’ll feel lucky to have this joyful show in your life
articles.description: Former Bake Off colleagues Prue Leith and Sandi Toksvig revisit the former’s home in a travelogue where they’re having the best time – as is everyone watching Sandi Toksvig is one of TV’s great pootlers. There are few sights as cheering as that of the tiny Dane, bundled up in a scarf, bimbling along a coastal path, or scurrying down a continental alleyway, like a Womble that’s just been chased out of a boulangerie after a misunderstanding over a bun. Said perambulations are generally accompanied by an accessory of some sort, an unofficial mascot for each of her pootle-based travelogues. In Sandi’s Great Riviera Rail Trip, for instance, it was a small suitcase. In Extraordinary Escapes With Sandi Toksvig it was Britain’s orangest cagoule. Now, in Prue and Sandi’s South African Adventure, it’s Prue Leith. Continue reading...

articles.title: Why are people captivated by this photo of a crowded Chris Bowen scowling? Is it the negative space?
articles.description: Australia’s climate change minister was president of negotiations at Cop31 in Turkey when it all went a bit sideways Blake, I was at the back of the huge plenary hall in Antalya on Sunday at the end of the UN climate summit that overran by two days. For about 20 minutes, you could see from the panic on the stage that it wasn’t going well. I only had an old iPhone, was a long way back, and remember thinking: “I’d love a long lens to see the expression on their faces.” Then came this incredible picture of Chris Bowen looking like all his Christmases had come at once and every present was a jumper he hates. Why can’t I stop looking at it? Continue reading...

articles.title: Farage preaches the Brexit gospel according to St Nige | John Crace
articles.description: Reform leader is happy to return to his anti-EU happy place, where the truth can be whatever you want it to be This feels like Nigel Farage’s happy place. It’s hardly a secret that he prefers his own company. His fellow Reform MPs are a necessary inconvenience at best. Muppets at worst. He can barely hide his misogyny for Sarah Pochin, having written her off as a pisshead. Nor does he have a much higher opinion of Richard Tice, Zia Yusuf and the others. But even Nige has worked out that when it comes to having a Potemkin alternative cabinet, he can’t realistically do everything himself. Only when it comes to Brexit, it seems, is Farage at his best as a one-man band. This is his battle. During Monday’s Commons statement, Andy Burnham said he didn’t want to keep “banging on about Europe”. But Nige most definitely does. Not least because the more he can talk about Brexit, the less people will criticise him for having no real plans for government. Most of his domestic policies collapse on contact with reality. As for foreign policy, he doesn’t have one. Unless you count having as little to do with the EU as possible. The Guardian’s year in review 2026. On Tuesday 1 December, join John

articles.title: Rayan Cherki magic denies Napoli but Manchester City’s struggles continue
articles.description: For reasons best known to those eyeing the pound signs, Manchester City gave a debut to a special rust-coloured kit in front of a nonplussed crowd. It was of a piece with their performance for most of a familiarly frustrating night that at least concluded with a shot of energy, the home side belatedly shaking off their torpor and ending the prospect of a triumphant return to the Etihad for Kevin De Bruyne. Despite the relief sparked by a fine equaliser by Rayan Cherki, who was rewarded for an insistent but hitherto fruitless evening’s endeavours when his angled shot flashed past Vanja Milinkovic-Savic, it was hard to see this as anything but a perfect snapshot of their autumn difficulties. Nobody could pretend City were up against crack opposition in a one-paced Napoli, who are eighth in Serie A and lack the brio of old, but they simply cannot keep the door shut and could not have quibbled about departing with a defeat. Continue reading...

articles.title: Dortmund’s Beier halts Arsenal charge after thunderbolt from Gyökeres
articles.description: Arsenal’s sky-high standards are slipping. For the second time in four days, Mikel Arteta’s side found themselves a goal up at half-time and apparently coasting toward victory, only for their opponents to rouse themselves and earn a deserved draw. After Newcastle on Saturday , this time it was an impressive Borussia Dortmund who became only the second side to take points off Arsenal in their past 15 group stage games in this competition. It could have been worse had an offside flag not ruled out Jobe ­Bellingham’s goal after Max Beier equalised a thunderbolt from Viktor Gyökeres. But the much-maligned Sweden striker was guilty of a glaring miss late on as Arsenal laid siege to Dortmund’s goal, racking up 30 shots by the final whistle. The German side had to hang on for a result that gave their travelling fans a night to remember, although Arteta admitted his players must be more clinical when Real Madrid and Jude Bellingham visit north London in a fortnight. Continue reading...

articles.title: Cowan-Dickie insists England will not let up after record triumph over All Blacks
articles.description: Hooker was involved in 2019 win against New Zealand ‘The way we trained today, I don’t see any complacency’ Luke Cowan-Dickie is adamant England will not let complacency creep in after their record win over the All Blacks , insisting they will not repeat the mistakes of the 2019 World Cup. Cowan-Dickie is one of three players, with Jamie George and Maro Itoje, who would claim a fourth career win for England against New Zealand on Saturday if Steve Borthwick’s side back up last weekend’s 37-12 victory at Twickenham. The Sale hooker was part of the squad who defeated the All Blacks in the 2019 World Cup semi-final in emphatic fashion and went into the final against South Africa as favourites. Eddie Jones’s side were comfortably outplayed by the Springboks , however, with Cowan-Dickie acknowledging that England failed to hit their emotional peak that day. Continue reading...

articles.title: Gukesh escapes time crisis to draw world chess championship opener with Sindarov
articles.description: Opening game ends in draw by repetition Defending champion plays white in Game 2 Read our move-by-move report of Game 1 Sindarov: ‘I can’t play games just for fun’ Indian chess star Gukesh Dommaraju held off Javokhir Sindarov amid a mounting time crisis on Tuesday, drawing the opening game of their eagerly awaited $2.5m world title match in 38 moves at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in the picturesque Geneva suburb of Cologny. After spending more than 36 minutes on a single move and much of the afternoon racing against the clock, the defending champion said the time he invested early helped him play faster as a drawish position sharpened and his minutes dwindled opposite the in-form Uzbek challenger . “When I got into the time trouble, I’d already thought about the next few moves,” Gukesh said. “And then the moves after that were pretty easy.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Democrat Victoria Broderick unseats eight-term Republican incumbent in Tennessee to win election
articles.description: Victory expands Democrats’ House majority, its largest advantage in three decades Democrat Victoria Broderick has won Tennessee’s fourth congressional district, unseating eight-term Republican incumbent Scott DesJarlais in one of the biggest House upsets of the cycle. The victory expands Democrats’ historic House majority in the 120th Congress to 259 seats, the party’s largest advantage in three decades , and flips a seat that Donald Trump carried by more than 20 points in 2024. Broderick, 34, a former technology and logistics professional who previously ran for Congress in 2024, told the Guardian in an interview before her race was called that she connected with constituents who had not voted in years and met Republicans concerned about affordability who appreciated the “integrity” she brought to the race. articles.title: Court Rules Democrats' Proxy Voting Unconstitutional, Putting Other Biden-Era Laws In Question
articles.description: Court Rules Democrats' Proxy Voting Unconstitutional, Putting Other Biden-Era Laws In Question A federal appeals court ruled Friday that the House violated the Constitution when it relied on pandemic-era proxy voting to pass former President Joe Biden's $1.7 trillion spending package almost four years ago. Joe Biden, 2022. (Mandel Ngan/Getty) The Fifth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in New Orleans split 9-8 in holding that the House lacked a constitutionally valid quorum when it approved the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023 in December 2022. The package cleared the chamber 225-201, according to the court's 58-page opinion. Of the members casting votes, 226 recorded both their votes and their presence by proxy , which left fewer than a majority of House members physically in the chamber. The majority concluded that the proxy arrangement violated Article I, Section 5 of the Constitution, which requires a majority of each chamber to form a quorum to do business. " 'Proxy presence' does not count ," Judge Cory Wilson, a Trump appointee, wrote for the majority. Some insiders think the control problem can be fixed; others want the companies to stop training new models entirely. articles.description: 'First Time This Far West': Russian Warship Suspected Of Blinding 140 Flights Off UK Coast A Russian warship shepherding three sanctioned cargo ships through the North Sea is suspected of jamming the satellite navigation of some 140 airliners on Nov. 9 , among them British Airways, easyJet and Ryanair flights out of London Heathrow, Manchester and Edinburgh, according to an analysis by aviation intelligence group Hexbird reported Tuesday by The Telegraph . Hexbird, run by aviation data analyst John Wiseman, traced the roughly 20-minute burst of interference to a radio transmitter over the North Sea about 190 miles off the English coast. By its count, around 40 of the affected aircraft were in or near UK-controlled airspace at the time. They included a Ryanair flight from Edinburgh to Rome, an easyJet flight from Manchester to Hurghada, Egypt, and a British Airways flight from London to Stockholm. The analysis found no operational effect on the flights; airliners carry backup navigation and pilots train for losing GPS. articles.title: The best Black Friday beauty deals I’d actually buy, from LED face masks to skincare staples
articles.description: We’ve rounded up the beauty and hair care offers that are actually worth it – all tried, tested and loved by us • The best Black Friday deals • The best Black Friday deals on winter essentials Few of us may be able to justify the cost of a big-ticket TV this Black Friday, but beauty is one area where we can usually afford a treat or two. Thank you, lipstick effect . It can feel like a no-brainer to stock up on our regular favourites and get a few Christmas presents crossed off the list while prices are lower. But deals do something funky to our brains. Retailers know how to lure us in, using big discounts and “selling fast” pop-ups that cause our typically rational brains to short circuit. Add a high-pressure countdown, and before you know it, you’ve been enticed into buying countless products you didn’t set out to buy. Impulse beauty buys are easy to regret later when you snap back into consciousness – not only because of the money you’ve spent, but also because of the waste they create. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Guardian view on Cop31: a just transition needs more than fine words | Editorial
articles.description: Petrostates blocked ambition while wealthy nations withheld cash support. The climate crisis demands the next UN summit turns promises into action In a negotiation the maxim is usually that no deal is better than a bad deal. But the failure of Cop31 in Turkey to get a climate pact – the first time this has happened in 17 years – should not be an excuse for leaving the planet with the damaging status quo. A hard bargain needs a credible route to agreement: by making commitments, seeking concessions and getting others to reciprocate. This did not happen at the weekend. Responsibility for the breakdown lay principally with petrostates resisting a transition away from fossil fuels and wealthy nations that are unwilling to finance it properly. With the US absent, the EU was foremost among the latter. European governments’ objection to fossil-fuel backsliding by a Saudi-Russian coalition was right, but they were wrong to rule out fresh EU funding for developing countries’ climate action. Despite their reservations, others – notably China and the African group – were prepared to accept a flawed package to keep multilateralism alive. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Guardian view on Andy Burnham’s EU intentions: undogmatic consensus building is a sensible strategy | Editorial
articles.description: On treacherous political terrain, the government is right to want to proceed with caution and at a pace of its own choosing During the 1980s and 90s, the French president of the European Commission, Jacques Delors, consciously pursued deeper EU integration via a gradualist approach that sought to minimise confrontation. Rather than focusing on ambitious end-goals, risking a showdown with some member states, Delors calculated that taking steps such as the creation of the internal market, in 1993, would eventually generate the momentum to go further. One thing would lead to another, in a logic of deeper union. Mindful of the unique capacity of the Brexit debate to divide and polarise, Andy Burnham appears, for the time being, to be adopting a version of this strategy. On Friday, the prime minister rightly hailed the signing of a reset deal with the EU on food exports, emissions trading and youth mobility as a “good day” for the UK. He then reiterated that further discussion was needed on finding the right long-term relationship with Brussels. Continue reading...

articles.title: Andy Burnham’s EU deal leaves Brexit open to question | Letters
articles.description: Stuart Finegan says the PM deserves credit for his practical steps to rebuild European relations, while Julian Roberts says the point of democracy is surely the right of the people to change their minds. Plus letters from Lindsay Bray , Helen Elliott and Nick Smith Your article ( Burnham seals trade and youth mobility deals in biggest step towards EU since Brexit, 20 November ) marks a welcome moment of political realism after years of denial about the consequences of Brexit. I wholeheartedly agree with Andy Burnham when he said: “This is a good day for Britain and this is a good day for Europe.” For years, the evidence has pointed in the same direction, that the UK economy is worse off as a result of Brexit. Trade barriers have increased, growth has suffered and businesses have been forced to navigate unnecessary bureaucracy. Many of the industries that Brexit supporters claimed would flourish have instead struggled. Fishing, farming, construction and touring musicians have all faced new obstacles, costs and restrictions. articles.title: A wake-up call for the UK government on wild birds | Letter
articles.description: Emma Phipps of SongBird Survival writes that the government must act now to save woodland and farmland species from extinction The Office for Environmental Protection’s finding that government departments are breaking the law by failing to protect wild birds should alarm us all ( UK government ‘breaking the law’ by not stopping decline of wild birds, 18 November ). The scale of bird declines in the UK is impossible to ignore, and songbirds are among the worst affected. The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs’ wild bird indicators show that nearly 70% of farmland songbird species have declined since 1970. Woodland songbirds are faring little better, with more than 30% of species in decline. Unfortunately, none of this comes as a surprise. Decades of monitoring by scientists and dedicated volunteers have shown that our wild birds are in trouble. Yet successive governments have failed to act with the urgency needed to halt these declines. Continue reading...

articles.title: If Trump, Xi and Putin are carving up the pudding, who gets the sixpence? | Letters
articles.description: Readers respond to an article by Rafael Behr on the Shenzhen summit, where the three world leaders met without a place at the table for Europe Rafael Behr ( Trump, Xi and Putin have a shared vision of global power – with no place for Europe, 18 November ) draws parallels between the Shenzhen summit and Winston Churchill, Joseph Stalin and Franklin D Roosevelt meeting at Yalta. I see it as bringing us a step closer to George Orwell’s Nineteen Eighty-Four, in which the world is divided into three superstates: Oceania, Eurasia and Eastasia. We already have the surveillance in the form of CCTV, facial-recognition technology and email trawling. Daily we witness the rewriting of history. We could be sleepwalking into a situation from which we will be unable to escape. Andy Fazakerley Irby, Wirral Continue reading...

articles.title: Sweden’s datacentre politics are more complicated than they appear | Letter
articles.description: There are distinct tensions over who controls, benefits from and gains access to natural and public resources, write James White and Nora Söderberg Steve Rose’s account of Sweden’s datacentre sector ( ‘Datacentres are deeply unpopular. Has Sweden made one we can all love?’, 12 November ) is a welcome reminder that digital infrastructure can be developed in more environmentally responsible ways. However, his suggestion that datacentres have become politically contentious elsewhere, “but here in Sweden, not so much”, is a misrepresentation. Consider the proposed Google datacentre development at Torsboda, near Sundsvall, which requires an enormous allocation of electricity and industrial land. The StoppaGoogle campaign , initiated by the regional political party Norrlandspartiet, has been vocal in challenging what this development will mean for electricity prices, employment and regional development. articles.title: Brioche armchairs, butter sculptures and edible chandeliers: meet the new food artists
articles.description: Culinary artists are turning fashion shows and design fairs into a feast for the eyes A pretty Venetian chandelier featuring delicate pink flowers and cascading blue leaves hangs from a ceiling. A hazy, warm light radiates from its tulip bulbs. Suddenly, a woman reaches up and snaps off one of the flower stems, giggling as she begins to nibble it. Welcome to the weird and wonderful world of Laila Gohar . The Egyptian-born, New York-based artist is part of a new wave of culinary artists blurring the lines between sustenance and spectacle, and this troupe have quickly become a firm fixture at fashion parties and design fairs, turning dining into a phenomenon and delight. Gohar describes the chandelier , made entirely from hand-spun sugar (including the silver chain that suspended it) as her “favourite thing she has done in recent history”. It joins a long list of extravagant yet still edible installations she has created, including lifesize armchairs made of brioche , an entire room constructed with Belgian chocolate and a four-metre-long mortadella that had to be lifted into the party’s venue using a crane. Continue reading...
